channel.title: sedzinfo · R tutorials
channel.description: Tutorials in R with the code on every page: psychometrics, adaptive testing, scale validation, statistics, machine learning and data visualisation with real data.

item.title: Multilevel (Hierarchical Linear) Models: Students Within Schools
item.description: Hierarchical linear (multilevel) models in R with nlme: 7,185 students in 160 schools, the ICC, random slopes, cross-level interactions and APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Hierarchical linear (multilevel) models in R with nlme: 7,185 students in 160 schools, the ICC, random slopes, cross-level interactions and APA reporting.

The problem: students inside schools

In 1982 the High School and Beyond survey gave a mathematics test to students of US high schools, public and Catholic. We use the classic subset of 7,185 students in 160 schools, and ask two questions:

  1. Students from richer families score higher in maths. Is that gap the same in every school?
  2. Do school characteristics, such as being a Catholic school or having richer students on average, change the scores and the gap?

The students are not 7,185 independent people. They come in groups: students of the same school share teachers, neighbourhoods and resources, so their scores are more alike than the scores of students from different schools. Ordinary regression ignores this, which causes two problems:

  • Wrong standard errors. Ordinary regression treats every student as new information, so it is far too confident about anything measured at the school level (section 4).
  • The wrong question. Ordinary regression gives one slope for everyone. The interesting questions here are about how the slopes differ between schools (sections 6 to 8).

A multilevel model handles both. It has one equation for the students (level 1) and one for the schools (level 2). The same models are also called hierarchical linear models (HLM), mixed (effects) models and random-effects models. They are not the same as “hierarchical regression” in the sense of entering predictors in blocks and testing \(\Delta R^2\), which has its own tutorial: Hierarchical Regression.

Code 
library(nlme)       # lme(): multilevel models (comes with R)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side

1. The data

The nlme package has the students in MathAchieve and the schools in MathAchSchool. We join them and give the columns short names:

Code 
students <- as.data.frame(MathAchieve)
hsb <- merge(students[, c("School", "Minority", "Sex", "SES", "MathAch")],
             MathAchSchool[, c("School", "Size", "Sector")], by = "School")
names(hsb) <- c("school", "minority", "sex", "ses", "math", "size", "sector")
hsb$school <- factor(hsb$school)
c(students = nrow(hsb), schools = nlevels(hsb$school))
students  schools 
    7185      160
Code 
table(sector = MathAchSchool$Sector)
sector
  Public Catholic 
      90       70
Code 
summary(as.numeric(table(hsb$school)))   # students per school
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  14.00   35.00   47.00   44.91   54.00   67.00
Variable Level Meaning
math student Mathematics achievement test score (from -2.8 to 25)
ses student Socio-economic status: a standardised composite of parental education, occupation and income
school school School identifier: the grouping variable
sector school Public or Catholic

Splitting SES into a school part and a student part

A student’s SES says two things: how well off their family is, and (through their classmates) how well off their school is. We split it in two:

Code 
hsb$ses_school <- ave(hsb$ses, hsb$school)       # the average SES of the student's school
hsb$ses_within <- hsb$ses - hsb$ses_school       # the student's SES compared with their schoolmates
head(hsb[, c("school", "sector", "ses", "ses_school", "ses_within", "math")])
  school sector    ses ses_school  ses_within   math
1   1224 Public -1.528  -0.434383 -1.09361702  5.876
2   1224 Public -0.588  -0.434383 -0.15361702 19.708
3   1224 Public -0.528  -0.434383 -0.09361702 20.349
4   1224 Public -0.668  -0.434383 -0.23361702  8.781
5   1224 Public -0.158  -0.434383  0.27638298 17.898
6   1224 Public  0.022  -0.434383  0.45638298  4.583
  • ses_school is the school mean SES: the same for every student of a school, so it is a school-level variable.
  • ses_within is the student’s SES centred within the school: positive for students better off than their schoolmates, negative for those worse off. Its mean in every school is 0.

This is called group-mean centring. Section 7 shows why it matters: the two parts have very different effects.

2. Look at the data

Eight schools, chosen at random, four of each sector. Each point is a student, and each line is an ordinary regression fitted to that school alone:

Code 
set.seed(3)
pick <- c(sample(unique(as.character(hsb$school[hsb$sector == "Public"])), 4),
          sample(unique(as.character(hsb$school[hsb$sector == "Catholic"])), 4))
few <- subset(hsb, school %in% pick)
few$label <- with(few, paste0(sector, " school ", school, "\n(", ave(math, school, FUN = length), " students)"))
ggplot(few, aes(ses, math)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, aes(colour = sector), linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~label, ncol = 4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Public = "#0082c8", Catholic = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "Maths score against family SES in eight schools", x = "SES", y = "maths score") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

All 160 schools, one line per school, drawn over the range of ses_within of its students:

Code 
per_school <- lmList(math ~ ses_within | school, data = hsb)   # an ordinary regression in every school
ols <- data.frame(school = rownames(coef(per_school)), coef(per_school), check.names = FALSE)
names(ols)[2:3] <- c("intercept", "slope")
ols$sector <- MathAchSchool$Sector[match(ols$school, MathAchSchool$School)]
ols$n      <- as.numeric(table(hsb$school)[ols$school])
rng <- aggregate(ses_within ~ school, hsb, range)
ols$x0 <- rng$ses_within[match(ols$school, rng$school), 1]
ols$x1 <- rng$ses_within[match(ols$school, rng$school), 2]
ggplot(ols) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x0, xend = x1, y = intercept + slope * x0, yend = intercept + slope * x1, colour = sector),
               alpha = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~sector) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Public = "#0082c8", Catholic = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "One regression line per school", x = "SES compared with schoolmates (ses_within)",
       y = "maths score") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Three things stand out:

  • The lines start at very different heights: some schools score much higher than others, whatever the SES of their students. The intercepts (the school averages) go from 4.2 to 19.7.
  • The slopes differ too: in some schools SES matters a lot, in others hardly at all (from -2 to 6.3). Some of this is real, and some is noise: a school of 14 students gives a very rough slope.
  • The Catholic lines look higher and flatter.

A multilevel model turns these impressions into estimates with honest uncertainty. We build it in steps, adding one idea at a time.

3. Step 0: the null model, or how much do schools differ?

The simplest multilevel model has no predictors. Student \(i\) in school \(j\):

\[\text{Level 1 (students):}\qquad \text{math}_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + r_{ij}, \qquad r_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]

\[\text{Level 2 (schools):}\qquad \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}, \qquad u_{0j} \sim N(0, \tau_{00})\]

  • \(\beta_{0j}\) is the average score of school \(j\).
  • \(\gamma_{00}\) (“gamma”) is the average over all schools: a fixed effect, one number for everyone.
  • \(u_{0j}\) is how far school \(j\) is from that average: a random effect, one per school. We do not estimate 160 separate numbers; we estimate their variance \(\tau_{00}\) (“tau”).
  • \(r_{ij}\) is how far student \(i\) is from their school’s average, with variance \(\sigma^2\).

Putting the two levels together gives one equation, which is what R fits: \(\text{math}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j} + r_{ij}\).

Code 
m0 <- lme(math ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
summary(m0)
Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML
  Data: hsb 
       AIC      BIC   logLik
  47122.79 47143.43 -23558.4
Random effects:
 Formula: ~1 | school
        (Intercept) Residual
StdDev:    2.934966 6.256862
Fixed effects:  math ~ 1 
               Value Std.Error   DF  t-value p-value
(Intercept) 12.63697 0.2443936 7025 51.70747       0
Standardized Within-Group Residuals:
        Min          Q1         Med          Q3         Max 
-3.06312473 -0.75387398  0.02670132  0.76062171  2.74262579 
Number of Observations: 7185
Number of Groups: 160

How to read the output

  • Linear mixed-effects model fit by REML: the estimation method. REML (restricted maximum likelihood) gives better variance estimates than ordinary maximum likelihood (ML). Section 9 explains when to switch to ML.
  • AIC, BIC, logLik: the fit of the model, used to compare models (lower AIC and BIC is better).
  • Random effects: the standard deviations of the random parts. (Intercept) is \(\sqrt{\tau_{00}}\), how much the school averages differ, and Residual is \(\sigma\), how much students differ within a school.
  • Fixed effects: the \(\gamma\)s, with standard errors, degrees of freedom, t and p, read like a regression table. Here there is only \(\gamma_{00}\) = 12.64, the average school score.
  • DF: lme() counts the degrees of freedom at the level of each predictor. Student-level effects get about as many as there are students, school-level effects about as many as there are schools (we will see 157 for them below).
  • Standardized Within-Group Residuals: a summary of the level-1 residuals; roughly symmetric around 0 is good.
  • Number of Observations and Number of Groups: 7185 students in 160 schools.

The intraclass correlation (ICC)

VarCorr() gives the variances:

Code 
VarCorr(m0)
school = pdLogChol(1) 
            Variance  StdDev  
(Intercept)  8.614025 2.934966
Residual    39.148322 6.256862
Code 
vc <- function(m) { v <- VarCorr(m); setNames(as.numeric(v[, "Variance"]), rownames(v)) }   # variances as numbers
tau00 <- vc(m0)["(Intercept)"]
sigma2 <- vc(m0)["Residual"]
icc <- unname(tau00 / (tau00 + sigma2))
icc
[1] 0.1803518

\[\text{ICC} = \frac{\tau_{00}}{\tau_{00} + \sigma^2} = \frac{8.61}{8.61 + 39.15} = 0.18\]

About 18% of the differences in maths scores lie between schools, and 82% between students of the same school. The ICC is also the correlation between the scores of two students of the same school. Any ICC above about 0.05 is a good reason for a multilevel model, and 0.18 is a lot.

4. What ignoring the schools does

Compare ordinary regression with a multilevel model that has the same two predictors, SES and sector:

Code 
fit_ols <- lm(math ~ ses + sector, data = hsb)
fit_mlm <- lme(math ~ ses + sector, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
se_ols <- summary(fit_ols)$coefficients[, "Std. Error"]
se_mlm <- summary(fit_mlm)$tTable[, "Std.Error"]
round(data.frame(estimate_ols = coef(fit_ols), se_ols, estimate_mlm = fixef(fit_mlm), se_mlm,
                 se_ratio = se_mlm / se_ols), 3)
               estimate_ols se_ols estimate_mlm se_mlm se_ratio
(Intercept)          11.793  0.106       11.719  0.228    2.149
ses                   2.949  0.098        2.375  0.105    1.078
sectorCatholic        1.935  0.152        2.101  0.341    2.237

The Catholic coefficient has a standard error 2.2 times larger in the multilevel model. Ordinary regression acts as if it had 7,185 independent pieces of information about Catholic schools. In fact there are only 160 schools, and the students of each school share most of what makes their school different.

The design effect says how much the clustering inflates the variance of an estimate. With \(\bar m\) students per school:

\[\text{design effect} = 1 + (\bar m - 1) \times \text{ICC} = 1 + (44.9 - 1) \times 0.18 = 8.9\]

so standard errors of school-level effects can be up to \(\sqrt{8.9} = 3\) times too small. (The ratio above is smaller because SES already explains part of the differences between schools.) Too-small standard errors mean confidence intervals that are too narrow and p values that are too small: findings that look stronger than they are.

5. Step 1: a student-level predictor

Now add the student’s SES, centred within the school:

\[\text{Level 1:}\qquad \text{math}_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1}\,\text{ses\_within}_{ij} + r_{ij}\]

\[\text{Level 2:}\qquad \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}, \qquad \beta_{1} = \gamma_{10}\]

The slope \(\beta_1\) is the same in every school for now (it has no \(u\)).

Code 
m1 <- lme(math ~ ses_within, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
summary(m1)$tTable
                Value Std.Error   DF  t-value      p-value
(Intercept) 12.636139 0.2444873 7024 51.68422 0.000000e+00
ses_within   2.191172 0.1086546 7024 20.16640 5.756752e-88
Code 
VarCorr(m1)
school = pdLogChol(1) 
            Variance  StdDev  
(Intercept)  8.672288 2.944875
Residual    37.010413 6.083618

Within a school, a student one SD higher in SES than their schoolmates scores about 2.19 points higher.

How much did SES explain? Compare the variances with the null model. The proportion by which a variance shrinks is the multilevel version of \(R^2\), one for each level:

Code 
c(sigma2_null = unname(sigma2), sigma2_step1 = unname(vc(m1)["Residual"]),
  level1_R2 = unname(1 - vc(m1)["Residual"] / sigma2))
 sigma2_null sigma2_step1    level1_R2 
 39.14832200  37.01041300   0.05461049

SES explains about 5.5% of the differences between students of the same school. The school variance \(\tau_{00}\) did not go down (8.67, against 8.61): it cannot, because ses_within has the same mean, 0, in every school. To explain why schools differ we need school-level predictors (section 7).

6. Step 2: random slopes, or does family background matter equally in every school?

Let the slope differ between schools:

\[\text{Level 1:}\qquad \text{math}_{ij} = \beta_{0j} + \beta_{1j}\,\text{ses\_within}_{ij} + r_{ij}\]

\[\text{Level 2:}\qquad \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + u_{0j}, \qquad \beta_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + u_{1j}\]

Now each school has its own slope \(\beta_{1j}\), spread around the average slope \(\gamma_{10}\) with variance \(\tau_{11}\). The intercepts and slopes may be correlated, with covariance \(\tau_{01}\). In R, random = ~ ses_within | school means “an intercept and a ses_within slope for every school”:

Code 
m2 <- lme(math ~ ses_within, random = ~ ses_within | school, data = hsb)
summary(m2)$tTable
                Value Std.Error   DF  t-value      p-value
(Intercept) 12.636193 0.2445038 7024 51.68097 0.000000e+00
ses_within   2.193196 0.1282586 7024 17.09980 2.936628e-64
Code 
VarCorr(m2)
school = pdLogChol(ses_within) 
            Variance   StdDev    Corr  
(Intercept)  8.6809690 2.9463484 (Intr)
ses_within   0.6939876 0.8330592 0.019 
Residual    36.7002004 6.0580690
Code 
tau11 <- unname(vc(m2)["ses_within"])
  • The average slope is still about 2.19.
  • The slopes vary with a standard deviation of \(\sqrt{\tau_{11}}\) = 0.83. If they are normally distributed, about 95% of schools have a slope between \(2.19 \pm 1.96 \times 0.83\), that is from 0.56 to 3.83. In practically every school richer students do better, but in some schools the gap is several times larger than in others.
  • Corr is the correlation of the intercepts and slopes, near 0 here: high-scoring schools do not have steeper or flatter slopes.

Is the slope variance real? A likelihood-ratio test

Compare the models with and without the random slope:

Code 
lrt <- anova(m1, m2)
lrt
   Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test  L.Ratio p-value
m1     1  4 46732.00 46759.51 -23362.00                        
m2     2  6 46726.23 46767.51 -23357.12 1 vs 2 9.761657  0.0076

The random slope adds two parameters (the variance \(\tau_{11}\) and the covariance \(\tau_{01}\)), and the likelihood-ratio test (L.Ratio) is 9.76, p = 0.0076. Both models have the same fixed effects, so comparing their REML fits is fine.

The p value is conservative (too large). The test asks whether \(\tau_{11} = 0\), and a variance cannot be negative, so 0 is at the edge of its possible values. The correct reference distribution is a 50:50 mixture of \(\chi^2\) with 1 and 2 degrees of freedom (Self & Liang, 1987; Stram & Lee, 1994):

Code 
LR <- lrt$L.Ratio[2]
c(p_naive = pchisq(LR, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE),
  p_mixture = 0.5 * pchisq(LR, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE) + 0.5 * pchisq(LR, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE))
    p_naive   p_mixture 
0.007590724 0.004686308

Either way, the SES gap does differ between schools.

The same sequence with one call: report_hlr()

The rwf package fits this sequence of models in one call: no random effect at all (an ordinary regression fitted with gls()), a random intercept, the predictor, and a random slope, compared step by step with likelihood-ratio tests. It uses ML (see section 9), so the numbers differ slightly from the REML fits above:

Code 
steps <- report_hlr(df = hsb, corlist = which(names(hsb) == "math"), factorlist = which(names(hsb) == "school"),
                    predictor = "ses_within", random_effect = "school")
steps[, c("model", "fixed", "random", "df", "AIC", "BIC", "logLik", "Test", "L.Ratio", "p.value")]
                       model             fixed               random df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test    L.Ratio       p.value
1                       base          math ~ 1                 <NA>  2 48103.73 48117.49 -24049.87                NA            NA
2           random_intercept          math ~ 1          ~1 | school  3 47121.81 47142.45 -23557.91 1 vs 2 983.921822 5.611909e-216
3 random_intercept_predictor math ~ ses_within          ~1 | school  4 46728.41 46755.93 -23360.21 2 vs 3 395.398363  5.529267e-88
4     random_intercept_slope math ~ ses_within ~ses_within | school  6 46722.98 46764.26 -23355.49 3 vs 4   9.433005  8.946412e-03

Read it row by row. The first test (1 vs 2) asks whether schools differ at all: an enormous likelihood ratio, the ICC of section 3 in test form. The second (2 vs 3) tests SES, the third (3 vs 4) the random slope.

What the model believes about each school: shrinkage

The model gives an estimate of the intercept and slope of every school (coef(m2)). They are not the same as the separate regressions of section 2:

Code 
eb <- coef(m2)                                   # the multilevel estimate for each school
ols$intercept_mlm <- eb[ols$school, "(Intercept)"]
ols$slope_mlm     <- eb[ols$school, "ses_within"]
g <- fixef(m2)
s1 <- ggplot(ols, aes(intercept, intercept_mlm, size = n)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = g[1], colour = "#E74C3C") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0082c8") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Intercepts (school averages)", x = "separate regression", y = "multilevel model", size = "students")
s2 <- ggplot(ols, aes(slope, slope_mlm, size = n)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = g[2], colour = "#E74C3C") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0082c8") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "SES slopes", x = "separate regression", y = "multilevel model", size = "students")
s1 + s2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")   # one legend for both panels
Code 
round(rbind(separate_regressions = range(ols$slope), multilevel_model = range(ols$slope_mlm)), 2)
                      [,1] [,2]
separate_regressions -2.02 6.27
multilevel_model      0.78 3.41

The multilevel estimates are pulled from the dashed diagonal (each school on its own) towards the red line (the average of all schools). This is called shrinkage, and the estimates are called empirical Bayes estimates. For a school average in the random-intercept model the formula is:

\[\hat\beta_{0j} = \lambda_j\,\bar y_j + (1 - \lambda_j)\,\hat\gamma_{00}, \qquad \lambda_j = \frac{\tau_{00}}{\tau_{00} + \sigma^2 / n_j}\]

\(\lambda_j\) is the reliability of school \(j\)’s own mean: close to 1 when the school has many students (its own mean is trustworthy), smaller when it has few. In the null model:

Code 
n_j <- as.numeric(table(hsb$school))
lambda <- tau00 / (tau00 + sigma2 / n_j)
round(c(smallest_school = min(lambda), median = median(lambda), largest_school = max(lambda)), 2)
smallest_school          median  largest_school 
           0.75            0.91            0.94

The slopes shrink much more than the intercepts. A slope estimated from 14 to 67 students is very noisy, and the slopes truly differ only a little (\(\sqrt{\tau_{11}}\) = 0.83), so most of the spread of the separate slopes (from -2 to 6.3) is noise. The model keeps the part it believes is real (from 0.8 to 3.4). The negative slopes of a few small schools were flukes.

7. Step 3: school-level predictors, within and between

Why do some schools score higher? Add two school-level predictors to the intercept equation: the school’s mean SES and its sector (Catholic = 1, public = 0):

\[\text{Level 2:}\qquad \beta_{0j} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{ses\_school}_j + \gamma_{02}\,\text{Catholic}_j + u_{0j}, \qquad \beta_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + u_{1j}\]

Code 
m3 <- lme(math ~ ses_within + ses_school + sector, random = ~ ses_within | school, data = hsb)
summary(m3)$tTable
                   Value Std.Error   DF   t-value      p-value
(Intercept)    12.063419 0.1991480 7024 60.575153 0.000000e+00
ses_within      2.194980 0.1284185 7024 17.092388 3.317645e-64
ses_school      5.246300 0.3683306  157 14.243455 4.423748e-30
sectorCatholic  1.372171 0.3055220  157  4.491234 1.365339e-05
Code 
VarCorr(m3)
school = pdLogChol(ses_within) 
            Variance   StdDev   Corr  
(Intercept)  2.3851744 1.544401 (Intr)
ses_within   0.7006628 0.837056 0.18  
Residual    36.7097503 6.058857
  • Catholic schools score 1.37 points higher than public schools with the same mean SES.
  • Note the DF: 157 for the school-level predictors, because there are 160 schools; 7024 for the student-level one.
  • The school variance fell from 8.68 to 2.39: school SES and sector explain 73% of the differences between school averages.

Within and between: two different SES effects

The two SES coefficients are very different:

  • Within a school, one SD more family SES goes with 2.19 points more.
  • Between schools, a school whose students are on average one SD better off scores 5.25 points higher.

The difference is the contextual effect: the extra score that comes from being in a better-off school, for two students with the same family SES. To get it directly, with its own standard error, use the uncentred SES together with the school mean (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002). There the school-mean coefficient is the contextual effect:

Code 
m_ctx <- lme(math ~ ses + ses_school, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
summary(m_ctx)$tTable
                Value Std.Error   DF  t-value      p-value
(Intercept) 12.683308 0.1493802 7024 84.90621 0.000000e+00
ses          2.191172 0.1086673 7024 20.16404 6.021818e-88
ses_school   3.675002 0.3776705  158  9.73071 7.953398e-18

Two students from equally well-off families differ by about 3.7 points if one attends a school whose mean SES is one unit higher.

What if we had not split SES? A model with the raw SES only gives a single slope:

Code 
m_raw <- lme(math ~ ses, random = ~ 1 | school, data = hsb)
round(c(raw_ses_slope = unname(fixef(m_raw)["ses"]), within = unname(fixef(m3)["ses_within"]),
        between = unname(fixef(m3)["ses_school"])), 2)
raw_ses_slope        within       between 
         2.39          2.19          5.25

The raw slope (2.39) is a blend of the within and the between effects, and answers neither question. Decide which question you are asking, and centre accordingly (Enders & Tofighi, 2007):

  • Group-mean centring (ses_within, plus ses_school at level 2) separates the within and the between effects. Use it when the student-level effect is the question, and for random slopes.
  • Grand-mean centring (SES minus the overall mean) keeps the blend but makes the intercept the score of an average student. Use it when the student-level predictor is only a control.

8. Step 4: cross-level interactions, or why do slopes differ?

Section 6 showed that the SES gap differs between schools. Can school characteristics explain why? Put the school predictors into the slope equation too:

\[\beta_{1j} = \gamma_{10} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{ses\_school}_j + \gamma_{12}\,\text{Catholic}_j + u_{1j}\]

Substituting into level 1 gives products of a student-level and a school-level variable: cross-level interactions.

\[\text{math}_{ij} = \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01}\,\text{ses\_school}_j + \gamma_{02}\,\text{Catholic}_j + \gamma_{10}\,\text{ses\_within}_{ij} + \gamma_{11}\,\text{ses\_school}_j \times \text{ses\_within}_{ij} + \gamma_{12}\,\text{Catholic}_j \times \text{ses\_within}_{ij} + u_{0j} + u_{1j}\,\text{ses\_within}_{ij} + r_{ij}\]

In R, ses_within * (ses_school + sector) writes all of these terms:

Code 
m4 <- lme(math ~ ses_within * (ses_school + sector), random = ~ ses_within | school, data = hsb)
summary(m4)$tTable
                              Value Std.Error   DF   t-value      p-value
(Intercept)               12.127931 0.1992951 7022 60.854147 0.000000e+00
ses_within                 2.945043 0.1555906 7022 18.928149 5.697836e-78
ses_school                 5.332878 0.3691743  157 14.445420 1.255094e-30
sectorCatholic             1.226578 0.3062783  157  4.004782 9.554485e-05
ses_within:ses_school      1.039249 0.2988794 7022  3.477152 5.098400e-04
ses_within:sectorCatholic -1.642680 0.2397649 7022 -6.851211 7.943710e-12
Code 
VarCorr(m4)
school = pdLogChol(ses_within) 
            Variance   StdDev    Corr  
(Intercept)  2.3797629 1.5426480 (Intr)
ses_within   0.1010237 0.3178422 0.391 
Residual    36.7211868 6.0598009
Code 
b4 <- fixef(m4)

Read the interactions as changes in the SES slope:

  • In a public school of average SES, the SES slope is 2.95.
  • In a Catholic school of average SES, it is 2.95 \(-\) 1.64 = 1.30: the gap between richer and poorer students is less than half as large.
  • In better-off schools the slope is steeper: 1.04 more per unit of school mean SES.

The slope variance fell from 0.70 to 0.10: sector and school SES explain 86% of the differences in SES slopes. Is any slope variance left?

Code 
m4_no_slope <- update(m4, random = ~ 1 | school)
anova(m4_no_slope, m4)
            Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test  L.Ratio p-value
m4_no_slope     1  8 46520.79 46575.82 -23252.39                        
m4              2 10 46523.66 46592.45 -23251.83 1 vs 2 1.124097    0.57

No (p = 0.57, and still clearly above .05 after halving it for the boundary). Once we know a school’s sector and mean SES, its SES slope is predictable; the remaining differences between schools are in their average scores. A simpler final model with a random intercept only would be defensible here; we keep the random slope to show the full model.

The model’s predictions show the pattern:

Code 
grid <- expand.grid(ses_within = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 50), sector = c("Public", "Catholic"),
                    ses_school = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5))
grid$sector <- factor(grid$sector, levels = levels(hsb$sector))
grid$math <- predict(m4, newdata = grid, level = 0)        # level = 0: the fixed effects, for a typical school
grid$school_ses <- factor(grid$ses_school, labels = c("poorer schools (mean SES -0.5)", "average schools (0)",
                                                      "richer schools (+0.5)"))
ggplot(grid, aes(ses_within, math, colour = sector)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(~school_ses) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Public = "#0082c8", Catholic = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "Predicted maths score: the SES gap is smaller in Catholic schools",
       x = "SES compared with schoolmates", y = "predicted maths score", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The Catholic advantage is largest for the students who are worse off than their schoolmates. For students well above their schoolmates the two sectors predict about the same score, and the lines cross. Richer schools (right) score higher in both sectors and have steeper lines.

A word of caution: students are not randomly assigned to Catholic schools. Families who choose them may differ in ways that SES does not capture, so these are associations, not proof that Catholic schools cause a smaller gap (Coleman et al., 1982, started a long debate about exactly this).

9. Comparing all the models

REML or ML? REML estimates the variances better, so report REML fits. But REML likelihoods can only be compared between models with the same fixed effects (as in section 6). To test fixed effects with a likelihood-ratio test, refit with method = "ML":

Code 
anova(update(m2, method = "ML"), update(m3, method = "ML"), update(m4, method = "ML"))
                          Model df      AIC      BIC    logLik   Test   L.Ratio p-value
update(m2, method = "ML")     1  6 46722.98 46764.26 -23355.49                         
update(m3, method = "ML")     2  8 46554.14 46609.18 -23269.07 1 vs 2 172.83591  <.0001
update(m4, method = "ML")     3 10 46516.43 46585.23 -23248.21 2 vs 3  41.71416  <.0001

Both steps improve the model a lot. All the models side by side:

Code 
models <- list("0: null" = m0, "1: + SES within" = m1, "2: + random slope" = m2,
               "3: + school SES, sector" = m3, "4: + cross-level interactions" = m4)
get_v <- function(m, name) { v <- vc(m); if (name %in% names(v)) unname(v[name]) else NA }
round(t(sapply(models, function(m) {
  ml <- update(m, method = "ML")
  c(tau00 = get_v(m, "(Intercept)"), tau11 = get_v(m, "ses_within"), sigma2 = get_v(m, "Residual"),
    parameters = attr(logLik(ml), "df"), AIC_ML = AIC(ml), BIC_ML = BIC(ml))
})), 2)
                              tau00 tau11 sigma2 parameters   AIC_ML   BIC_ML
0: null                        8.61    NA  39.15          3 47121.81 47142.45
1: + SES within                8.67    NA  37.01          4 46728.41 46755.93
2: + random slope              8.68  0.69  36.70          6 46722.98 46764.26
3: + school SES, sector        2.39  0.70  36.71          8 46554.14 46609.18
4: + cross-level interactions  2.38  0.10  36.72         10 46516.43 46585.23

And the variance each step explained, against the model before it at the same level:

Variance From To Explained by Share explained
\(\sigma^2\), students within schools 39.15 (step 0) 37.01 (step 1) student SES 5.5%
\(\tau_{00}\), school averages 8.68 (step 2) 2.39 (step 3) school SES and sector 73%
\(\tau_{11}\), SES slopes 0.70 (step 3) 0.10 (step 4) school SES and sector 86%

10. Checking the assumptions

A multilevel model assumes, at each level, normally distributed random parts with constant variance: the student residuals \(r_{ij}\) and the school effects \(u_{0j}\) and \(u_{1j}\).

Code 
d <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(m4), residual = resid(m4, type = "normalized"))
re <- ranef(m4)
qq <- function(x, title) ggplot(data.frame(x = x), aes(sample = x)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#0082c8") + stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = title, x = "normal quantiles", y = "sample quantiles")
d1 <- ggplot(d, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#E74C3C") +
  labs(title = "Student residuals against fitted", x = "fitted maths score", y = "standardised residual")
(d1 + qq(d$residual, "Student residuals")) / (qq(re[, "(Intercept)"], "School intercepts (u0)") +
                                              qq(re[, "ses_within"], "School slopes (u1)"))
  • Student residuals against fitted: a band around 0 with no curve in it. Its sharp upper edge on the right is the ceiling of the test: the top score is 25, so a student predicted to score 20 cannot be more than 5 points above the prediction. The lower edge on the left is the floor, for the same reason.
  • Student residuals: close to the line in the middle; the tails are shorter than those of a normal distribution, again because of the floor and the ceiling. With 7,185 students, this hardly affects the estimates.
  • School intercepts and slopes: close to the line. With 160 schools that is what matters for the level-2 estimates. The slopes are strongly shrunken (section 6), so their spread is small.

11. The same models in lme4

The lme4 package is the other common choice. Its lmer() writes the random part inside the formula, in brackets:

Code 
m4_lmer <- lme4::lmer(math ~ ses_within * (ses_school + sector) + (ses_within | school), data = hsb)
round(cbind(nlme = fixef(m4), lme4 = lme4::fixef(m4_lmer)), 3)
                            nlme   lme4
(Intercept)               12.128 12.128
ses_within                 2.945  2.945
ses_school                 5.333  5.333
sectorCatholic             1.227  1.227
ses_within:ses_school      1.039  1.039
ses_within:sectorCatholic -1.643 -1.643

The estimates are the same. Translation table:

Model nlme lme4
Random intercept lme(y ~ x, random = ~ 1 | g) lmer(y ~ x + (1 | g))
Random intercept and slope lme(y ~ x, random = ~ x | g) lmer(y ~ x + (x | g))
ML instead of REML method = "ML" REML = FALSE
Variances VarCorr(m) VarCorr(m)
School-level estimates coef(m), ranef(m) coef(m), ranef(m)

lmer() does not print p values for the fixed effects, because their degrees of freedom are not obvious. The lmerTest package adds them (with Satterthwaite’s approximation); lme() gives them directly, as above.

12. Reporting the results in APA style

A report (APA 7th edition) should give the structure of the data, the ICC, how the model was built, the fixed effects with their uncertainty, the variance components, and the tests of the random effects. We collect the numbers from the R objects:

Code 
tt  <- summary(m4)$tTable
ci  <- intervals(m4, which = "fixed")$fixed
v4  <- vc(m4)
lr_slope <- anova(m1, m2)
ml_test  <- anova(update(m3, method = "ML"), update(m4, method = "ML"))
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^0", "", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))

Method (data analysis):

Mathematics achievement scores of 7,185 students nested in 160 high schools (70 Catholic, 90 public; 14 to 67 students per school) were analysed with two-level linear models (students within schools), estimated by restricted maximum likelihood in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the nlme package. Student socio-economic status (SES) was centred on the school mean, and the school mean SES was entered as a school-level predictor. Models were built in steps: a null model, student SES, a random SES slope, school-level predictors (mean SES and sector), and cross-level interactions. Fixed effects were compared with likelihood-ratio tests of maximum-likelihood fits.

Results:

In the null model, 18% of the variance in mathematics achievement lay between schools (ICC = .18). Students with higher SES than their schoolmates scored higher, and this within-school SES slope varied between schools, χ²(2) = 9.76, p = .008. In the final model (Table 1), students in Catholic schools scored higher than students in public schools with the same mean SES, b = 1.23, 95% CI [0.62, 1.83], and school mean SES was strongly related to achievement, b = 5.33, 95% CI [4.60, 6.06]. The within-school SES slope was 2.95 in public schools of average SES, smaller in Catholic schools, b = -1.64, 95% CI [-2.11, -1.17], and larger in schools with higher mean SES, b = 1.04, 95% CI [0.45, 1.63]. Adding the cross-level interactions improved the model, χ²(2) = 41.71, p < .001, and reduced the slope variance by 86%.

Table 1

Two-Level Model of Mathematics Achievement

Effect b SE df t p 95% CI
Fixed effects
Intercept 12.13 0.20 7022 60.85 < .001 [11.74, 12.52]
Student SES (within school) 2.95 0.16 7022 18.93 < .001 [2.64, 3.25]
School mean SES 5.33 0.37 157 14.45 < .001 [4.60, 6.06]
Catholic (vs public) 1.23 0.31 157 4.00 < .001 [0.62, 1.83]
Student SES × school mean SES 1.04 0.30 7022 3.48 < .001 [0.45, 1.63]
Student SES × Catholic -1.64 0.24 7022 -6.85 < .001 [-2.11, -1.17]
Random effects
Intercept variance (τ00) 2.38
SES slope variance (τ11) 0.10
Residual variance (σ²) 36.72

Note. N = 7,185 students in 160 schools. Restricted maximum likelihood estimates. Student SES is centred on the school mean. Variances are given in the b column.

Points to remember:

  • Report the ICC of the null model, and the number of groups and of observations per group.
  • Say how the predictors were centred: it changes what the coefficients mean.
  • Report the variance components, not only the fixed effects, and how the random slopes were tested (and that the test is conservative, or corrected for the boundary).
  • Say whether the likelihood-ratio tests of fixed effects used ML fits.
  • Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("nlme") in R give the exact references.

13. Summary

When Observations come in groups (students in schools, employees in teams, patients in hospitals, repeated measurements in people)
Why not OLS Observations in a group are alike (ICC > 0), so standard errors are too small, especially for group-level predictors
Step 0: null model lme(y ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | g); ICC = \(\tau_{00} / (\tau_{00} + \sigma^2)\)
Level-1 predictors Centre within the group to get the within effect; add the group mean for the between effect
Random slopes random = ~ x | g; test with a likelihood-ratio test, which is conservative at the boundary
Level-2 predictors Explain the differences between group averages (less \(\tau_{00}\))
Cross-level interactions x * w, with x at level 1 and w at level 2: explain why slopes differ (less \(\tau_{11}\))
Estimation REML to report; ML to compare models with different fixed effects
Group estimates Shrunk towards the average, more so for small groups and noisy slopes
R nlme::lme(), or lme4::lmer() with lmerTest for p values; rwf::report_hlr() for the step-by-step sequence

References

Bates, D., Mächler, M., Bolker, B., & Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. Journal of Statistical Software, 67(1), 1–48.

Coleman, J. S., Hoffer, T., & Kilgore, S. (1982). High school achievement: Public, Catholic, and private schools compared. Basic Books.

Enders, C. K., & Tofighi, D. (2007). Centering predictor variables in cross-sectional multilevel models: A new look at an old issue. Psychological Methods, 12(2), 121–138.

Hox, J. J., Moerbeek, M., & van de Schoot, R. (2018). Multilevel analysis: Techniques and applications (3rd ed.). Routledge.

Pinheiro, J. C., & Bates, D. M. (2000). Mixed-effects models in S and S-PLUS. Springer.

Pinheiro, J., Bates, D., & R Core Team. (2026). nlme: Linear and nonlinear mixed effects models (R package version 3.1-172). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=nlme

Raudenbush, S. W., & Bryk, A. S. (2002). Hierarchical linear models: Applications and data analysis methods (2nd ed.). Sage.

Self, S. G., & Liang, K.-Y. (1987). Asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators and likelihood ratio tests under nonstandard conditions. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82(398), 605–610.

Snijders, T. A. B., & Bosker, R. J. (2012). Multilevel analysis: An introduction to basic and advanced multilevel modeling (2nd ed.). Sage.

Stram, D. O., & Lee, J. W. (1994). Variance components testing in the longitudinal mixed effects model. Biometrics, 50(4), 1171–1177.

See also

  • rwf: the R package behind report_hlr() on this page

This post first appeared on Worked Examples in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Hierarchical Regression: Does Beauty Predict Teaching Evaluations?
item.description: Hierarchical (blockwise) regression in R with real data: do better-looking instructors get better evaluations? R² change, F-change, order effects, APA reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Hierarchical (blockwise) regression in R with real data: do better-looking instructors get better evaluations? R² change, F-change, order effects, APA reporting.

The question: does beauty matter over and above everything else?

At the end of every term, students at the University of Texas at Austin rated their courses from 1 (very unsatisfactory) to 5 (excellent). For 463 courses taught between 2000 and 2002, economists Daniel Hamermesh and Amy Parker also asked six students to rate the physical appearance of each instructor from their photograph. Their question: do better-looking instructors get better evaluations (Hamermesh & Parker, 2005)?

A simple correlation is not enough to answer it. Beauty might go together with other things that also affect evaluations: age, gender, the kind of course, the size of the class. The real question is one of incremental validity:

Does beauty predict teaching evaluations over and above who the instructor is and what they teach?

Hierarchical regression answers exactly this kind of question. We enter the predictors in blocks, in an order decided in advance, and after each block we ask how much more of the variance of the outcome the model explains. That increase is the R² change, \(\Delta R^2\), and the F-change test tells us whether it is larger than chance.

The predictor of interest goes in last, so it gets credit only for what the earlier blocks cannot explain. If beauty still adds something after everything else, that is strong evidence that it matters on its own.

A note on the name. “Hierarchical” here means the order in which blocks of predictors enter the model. It has nothing to do with hierarchical linear models, also called multilevel or mixed models, which are for data nested in groups (students in schools, courses in instructors). Those have their own tutorial: Multilevel Models. We will meet the nesting issue in section 8, because these data have it too.

Code 
library(AER)        # the data: TeachingRatings
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots together
library(car)        # vif(): checks multicollinearity
library(sandwich)   # vcovCL(): cluster-robust standard errors (section 8)
library(lmtest)     # coeftest() and waldtest() with those standard errors
library(ggfortify)  # needed by rwf's report_regression() for its diagnostic plots (section 7)

1. The data

Code 
data("TeachingRatings", package = "AER")
tr <- TeachingRatings
c(courses = nrow(tr), instructors = length(unique(tr$prof)))
    courses instructors 
        463          94
Variable Meaning
eval The course’s average evaluation, from 1 (very unsatisfactory) to 5 (excellent)
beauty The instructor’s appearance, rated by six students from a photograph and averaged, shifted to a mean of 0
gender, minority, native, age The instructor: female or male, from a minority (non-Caucasian) or not, native English speaker or not, age in years
tenure Is the instructor on the tenure track?
division An upper-division course, or a lower-division one (mainly large first- and second-year courses)
credits A single-credit elective (yoga, aerobics, dance) or a regular course
allstudents The number of students enrolled
prof Which of the 94 instructors taught the course

We code each yes/no variable as a 0/1 dummy with a clear name, so that every coefficient says what it compares. Age goes in decades, so that its coefficient is not a tiny number per year. Class size is very skewed (8 to 581 students), so we use its base-2 logarithm: one unit more means twice as many students.

Code 
d <- data.frame(
  eval           = tr$eval,
  female         = as.integer(tr$gender == "female"),   # 1 = female instructor
  minority       = as.integer(tr$minority == "yes"),    # 1 = minority (non-Caucasian)
  non_native     = as.integer(tr$native == "no"),       # 1 = not a native English speaker
  age            = tr$age / 10,                         # in decades: +1 = ten years older
  tenure_track   = as.integer(tr$tenure == "yes"),      # 1 = on the tenure track
  lower_division = as.integer(tr$division == "lower"),  # 1 = lower-division course
  single_credit  = as.integer(tr$credits == "single"),  # 1 = single-credit elective
  log2_size      = log2(tr$allstudents),                # +1 = class twice as large
  beauty         = tr$beauty,
  prof           = tr$prof)
round(sapply(d[, 1:10], function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x), min = min(x), max = max(x))), 2)
     eval female minority non_native  age tenure_track lower_division single_credit log2_size beauty
mean 4.00   0.42     0.14       0.06 4.84         0.78           0.34          0.06      5.15   0.00
sd   0.55   0.49     0.35       0.24 0.98         0.41           0.47          0.23      1.22   0.79
min  2.10   0.00     0.00       0.00 2.90         0.00           0.00          0.00      3.00  -1.45
max  5.00   1.00     1.00       1.00 7.30         1.00           1.00          1.00      9.18   1.97

For the dummies, the mean is the share of courses with a 1: for example, 42% of the courses were taught by women and 6% were single-credit electives. The average evaluation is 4.00 (SD = 0.55): students were generally satisfied.

Hierarchical regression compares models fitted to the same people. If some variables had missing values, each model would drop different rows and the R² values would not be comparable. These data have none, but in your own data remove incomplete rows first, e.g. d <- na.omit(d[, variables_of_all_blocks]).

2. Look at the data

Code 
r_beauty <- cor(d$beauty, d$eval)
p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(beauty, eval)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#E74C3C", fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.15) +
  labs(title = sprintf("Better-looking instructors get somewhat better evaluations (r = %.2f)", r_beauty),
       x = "beauty rating (0 = average)", y = "course evaluation (1 to 5)")
predictors <- c("female", "minority", "non_native", "age", "tenure_track",
                "lower_division", "single_credit", "log2_size", "beauty")
cors <- data.frame(predictor = factor(predictors, levels = rev(predictors)),
                   with_eval = sapply(d[predictors], cor, y = d$eval))
p2 <- ggplot(cors, aes(with_eval, predictor, fill = with_eval > 0)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#0082c8", `FALSE` = "#E74C3C"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "Correlation of each predictor with the evaluation", x = "correlation", y = NULL)
p1 / p2

Beauty correlates 0.19 with the evaluations, so it explains \(r^2\) = 3.6% of their variance on its own. Single-credit electives get the best evaluations; female, non-native and tenure-track instructors, and larger classes, get lower ones. Several of these predictors also correlate with beauty, which is why we need a model that holds them constant.

3. The plan: three blocks, chosen in advance

Step Block Predictors Why here
1 Who the instructor is female, minority, non_native, age Fixed before any teaching starts, so nothing else can cause them
2 The job and the course tenure_track, lower_division, single_credit, log2_size What and whom they teach, and on which contract
3 Appearance beauty The predictor of interest: entered last, so it must explain something the first two blocks cannot

The order comes from theory and the research question, decided before looking at the results. Common rules: background variables and things that come first in time go first, control variables go before the predictors of interest, and the predictor whose added value you want to test goes last.

This is the opposite of stepwise regression, where the computer adds or drops predictors according to their p values. Stepwise selection capitalises on chance, and its p values and R² are too optimistic. In hierarchical regression you decide the order, and the data only answer the question you asked.

4. Fit the three models and test each step

Code 
m0 <- lm(eval ~ 1, data = d)                                                        # no predictors: R² = 0
m1 <- lm(eval ~ female + minority + non_native + age, data = d)                     # step 1
m2 <- update(m1, . ~ . + tenure_track + lower_division + single_credit + log2_size) # step 2: + block 2
m3 <- update(m2, . ~ . + beauty)                                                    # step 3: + beauty

update(m1, . ~ . + ...) means: the same model as m1, with these predictors added.

The formulas

For a model with \(k\) predictors fitted to \(n\) cases:

  • R², the share of the variance of the outcome the model explains: \(R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{RSS}{TSS}\), where \(RSS = \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\) is what the model leaves unexplained and \(TSS = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2\) is the total.
  • Adjusted R² corrects R² for the number of predictors, since adding any predictor, even pure noise, raises R² a little: \(R^2_{adj} = 1 - (1 - R^2)\dfrac{n - 1}{n - k - 1}\)
  • R² change from a smaller model (1) to a larger one (2): \(\Delta R^2 = R^2_2 - R^2_1\)
  • F-change, the test of \(\Delta R^2\), where \(\Delta k\) is the number of predictors added and \(k_2\) the number in the larger model:

\[F = \frac{\Delta R^2 / \Delta k}{(1 - R^2_2) / (n - k_2 - 1)}, \qquad \text{with } \Delta k \text{ and } n - k_2 - 1 \text{ degrees of freedom}\]

The top is the variance explained by the new block, per predictor added. The bottom is the variance still unexplained, per remaining degree of freedom. If the new block were useless, the two would be about equal and \(F\) would be close to 1.

  • Effect size of the change, Cohen’s \(f^2 = \dfrac{\Delta R^2}{1 - R^2_2}\): about .02 is small, .15 medium and .35 large (Cohen, 1988).

The steps by hand

Code 
n <- nrow(d)
models <- list(m0, m1, m2, m3)
k_of <- function(m) length(coef(m)) - 1                     # number of predictors
steps <- do.call(rbind, lapply(2:4, function(i) {
  small <- models[[i - 1]]; big <- models[[i]]
  r2_small <- summary(small)$r.squared
  r2_big   <- summary(big)$r.squared
  delta    <- r2_big - r2_small
  dk       <- k_of(big) - k_of(small)
  df2      <- n - k_of(big) - 1
  F_change <- (delta / dk) / ((1 - r2_big) / df2)
  data.frame(step = i - 1, k = k_of(big), r2 = r2_big, adj_r2 = summary(big)$adj.r.squared,
             delta_r2 = delta, F_change = F_change, df1 = dk, df2 = df2,
             p = pf(F_change, dk, df2, lower.tail = FALSE), f2 = delta / (1 - r2_big))
}))
steps$block <- c("1: who the instructor is", "2: + the job and the course", "3: + beauty")
format(steps[, c("block", "k", "r2", "adj_r2", "delta_r2", "F_change", "df1", "df2", "p", "f2")], digits = 3)
                        block k     r2 adj_r2 delta_r2 F_change df1 df2        p     f2
1    1: who the instructor is 4 0.0527 0.0444   0.0527     6.37   4 458 5.40e-05 0.0556
2 2: + the job and the course 8 0.1268 0.1114   0.0741     9.63   4 454 1.76e-07 0.0848
3                 3: + beauty 9 0.1726 0.1562   0.0458    25.10   1 453 7.81e-07 0.0554
Code 
bars <- data.frame(model = factor(rep(steps$block, 1:3), levels = steps$block),
                   block = factor(c(steps$block[1], steps$block[1:2], steps$block[1:3]), levels = steps$block),
                   value = c(steps$delta_r2[1], steps$delta_r2[1:2], steps$delta_r2[1:3]))
ggplot(bars, aes(model, value, fill = block)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_text(data = steps, aes(x = block, y = r2, label = sprintf("R² = %.3f\nΔR² = %.3f", r2, delta_r2)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, vjust = -0.3, size = 3.2, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#95A5A6", "#f39c12", "#E74C3C"), labels = c("block 1", "block 2", "beauty")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.22), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Variance of the evaluations explained, step by step", x = NULL, y = "R²", fill = NULL)

Step by step:

  1. Who the instructor is explains 5.3% of the variance of the evaluations, F(4, 458) = 6.37, p < .001.
  2. The job and the course add another 7.4%, F(4, 454) = 9.63, p < .001.
  3. Beauty adds 4.6% more, F(1, 453) = 25.1, p < .001, \(f^2\) = 0.055, a small effect by Cohen’s labels. Beauty predicts evaluations even after all eight other predictors have had their say.

Altogether the model explains 17.3% (adjusted 15.6%). Most of what makes a course well rated is not in these data, which is normal for something as complex as teaching.

How to read it: Res.Df and RSS are the residual degrees of freedom and the residual sum of squares of each model. Df is the number of predictors added, Sum of Sq how much the residual sum of squares went down, and F and Pr(>F) are the F-change and its p value.

The last line is the same, but the F for step 2 is now 10.14 instead of 9.63. With several models, anova() divides every comparison by the unexplained variance of the largest model (here m3), not of the model at that step. Both are valid tests. The pairwise version matches the F-change formula and SPSS; say which one you report.

One predictor: ΔR² is its squared semipartial correlation

When a step adds a single predictor, two shortcuts hold:

  • \(\Delta R^2\) equals the squared semipartial correlation \(sr^2\): the squared correlation between the outcome and the part of beauty that the other eight predictors cannot predict.
  • The F-change equals the square of beauty’s t value in the final model.
Code 
beauty_unique <- resid(lm(beauty ~ female + minority + non_native + age + tenure_track +
                            lower_division + single_credit + log2_size, data = d))   # beauty, minus what the others predict
t_beauty <- summary(m3)$coefficients["beauty", "t value"]
c(delta_r2 = steps$delta_r2[3], semipartial_squared = cor(d$eval, beauty_unique)^2,
  F_change = steps$F_change[3], t_squared = t_beauty^2)
           delta_r2 semipartial_squared            F_change           t_squared 
         0.04584582          0.04584582         25.10107854         25.10107854

So \(\Delta R^2\) for a single predictor is the share of the variance of the evaluations that only beauty explains.

How to read the output

Part Meaning
Estimate \(b\): the change in the evaluation for one unit more of the predictor, holding all the other predictors constant. For a 0/1 dummy, the difference between the two groups
Std. Error How uncertain the estimate is
t value Estimate / Std. Error
Pr(>|t|) The chance of a t this large if the true effect were 0
Residual standard error The typical distance of an evaluation from the model’s prediction, in evaluation points
Multiple R-squared, Adjusted R-squared R² and adjusted R² of the final model, as in our table
F-statistic Tests all nine predictors together against the model with none
  • (Intercept) is the predicted evaluation when every predictor is 0: a male, native, non-minority instructor aged 0, teaching one student. It is needed for the predictions but means nothing by itself.
  • beauty: 0.159 points per unit of beauty. One standard deviation of beauty (0.79) is worth 0.13 points, and the gap between the least and the best-looking instructor in the data is 0.55 points, about one standard deviation of the evaluations.
  • female: courses taught by women are rated 0.20 points lower than comparable courses taught by men.
  • single_credit: single-credit electives are rated 0.55 points higher.
  • log2_size: each doubling of the class costs 0.06 points.
  • non_native and minority instructors are rated 0.25 and 0.18 points lower; age, tenure track and division add nothing once the rest is held constant.

These are associations in observational data. Better-looking people may also be more confident or more practised speakers, so the coefficient says that beauty predicts evaluations, not that it causes them.

Standardised coefficients

The b’s are in different units (decades, doublings of the class, rating points), so they cannot be compared with each other. A standardised coefficient \(\beta\) puts every predictor in standard deviations: \(\beta = b \cdot \dfrac{SD_x}{SD_y}\), the change in the evaluation, in SDs, for one SD more of the predictor.

Code

ci <- confint(m3)[predictors, ]
betas <- data.frame(predictor = factor(predictors, levels = rev(predictors)),
                    b = coef(m3)[predictors], beta = coef(m3)[predictors] * sd_ratio,
                    low = ci[, 1] * sd_ratio, high = ci[, 2] * sd_ratio)
round(betas[, -1], 3)

Beauty (\(\beta\) = 0.23) and single-credit electives (\(\beta\) = 0.23) are the strongest predictors. For 0/1 dummies, a “one SD change” is an odd idea, so many authors report \(\beta\) only for continuous predictors and \(b\) for dummies.

6. The order matters

What if we had entered beauty first? Its share would then be its squared correlation with the evaluations. Entered last, it is its squared semipartial correlation. Here is that comparison for every predictor:

order_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(predictors, function(v) {
  alone   <- summary(lm(reformulate(v, "eval"), data = d))$r.squared            # entered first: r²
  without <- summary(update(m3, as.formula(paste(". ~ . -", v))))$r.squared
  data.frame(predictor = v, entered_first = alone, entered_last = full_r2 - without)   # entered last: sr²
}))

  geom_col(width = 0.6, position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.3f", value)), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5, reverse = TRUE), size = 3.2) +

  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
# (b) each predictor entered first (r²) and last (sr²)
order_tab$predictor <- factor(order_tab$predictor, levels = rev(predictors))

  geom_segment(aes(x = entered_first, xend = entered_last, yend = predictor), colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = entered_first, colour = "entered first (r²)"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = entered_last, colour = "entered last (sr²)"), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("entered first (r²)" = "#0082c8", "entered last (sr²)" = "#E74C3C")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "(b) Variance each predictor explains, entered first or last",
       x = "share of the variance of the evaluations", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
pa / pb

Two things happen:

  • Shared variance shrinks a predictor’s share. Tenure track explains 1.7% of the variance alone, but only 0.1% when entered last. What it explains, the other predictors explain too: tenure-track instructors rarely teach the well-rated single-credit electives (r = -0.29) and teach larger classes (r = 0.16). In hierarchical regression shared variance goes to the block that enters first. Division shows the same, because the single-credit electives are lower-division courses (r = 0.33), and so does native language.
  • Suppression enlarges it. Beauty explains 3.6% alone, but 4.6% entered last. Better-looking instructors are more often women (r = 0.13), teach somewhat larger classes (r = 0.07) and fewer single-credit electives (r = -0.08): all of these go with lower evaluations, so they hide part of beauty’s effect in the simple correlation. Holding them constant uncovers it. Gender, minority and class size grow for similar reasons.

That is why the order must be decided before the analysis and reported with the results: with correlated predictors, the credit each block gets depends on where it enters. The total R² does not change (panel a). Entering the predictor of interest last is the conservative choice: it gets credit only for what nothing else explains.

7. Checking the assumptions

The F-change tests and the standard errors assume that the residuals have constant variance, are roughly normal, contain no extreme cases with undue influence, and are independent of each other; that the relationships are linear; and that the predictors are not too strongly correlated. report_regression() of the rwf package collects the usual checks for an lm model: diagnostic plots, standardised coefficients, VIFs, an outlier test and more. It also prints a long text report, which we capture here, and keep only the parts we need:

Code 
set.seed(1)    # its Durbin-Watson test uses random resampling
invisible(capture.output(diag_m3 <- report_regression(m3, plot_diagnostics = TRUE)))
Panel What to look for Here
Residuals vs Fitted No curve and no funnel shape Flat, but the residuals are cut off at the top: no course can be rated above 5
Normal Q-Q Points on the line A longer lower tail: a few courses were rated much lower than predicted
Scale-Location A flat line: constant variance Roughly flat
Cook’s distance No case far above the others (values above 1 are a concern) The largest is 0.05
Residuals vs Leverage, Cook’s dist vs Leverage No case with both high leverage and a large residual None
Code 
data.frame(predictor = predictors, vif = round(diag_m3$vif$vif, 2), tolerance = round(diag_m3$vif$tolerance, 2))
       predictor  vif tolerance
1         female 1.14      0.88
2       minority 1.25      0.80
3     non_native 1.15      0.87
4            age 1.24      0.81
5   tenure_track 1.20      0.84
6 lower_division 1.22      0.82
7  single_credit 1.34      0.75
8      log2_size 1.11      0.90
9         beauty 1.12      0.89
Code 
diag_m3$outlier_test   # the most extreme studentised residual, with a Bonferroni-corrected p value
    rstudent            p   bonf.p signif cutoff
99 -3.591951 0.0003642181 0.168633  FALSE   0.05
  • Multicollinearity: the VIF (variance inflation factor) says how much a coefficient’s variance grows because the predictor correlates with the others. All are below 1.4, far from the usual warning level of 5 to 10.
  • Outliers: the most extreme residual is not significant after the Bonferroni correction (bonf.p = 0.17).
  • Normality: the skew comes from the ceiling at 5. With 463 cases, the tests of the coefficients are robust to it.

The assumption that these plots cannot check is independence, and these data break it.

8. A caveat: 463 courses, but only 94 instructors

Each instructor taught between 1 and 13 of the courses, and their beauty rating is the same in all of them. The plot shows every course as a point and joins the courses of the same instructor:

Code 
ggplot(d, aes(beauty, eval, group = prof)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(colour = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6) +
  labs(title = "Each vertical strip is one instructor and their courses",
       x = "beauty rating of the instructor", y = "course evaluation")

Courses of the same instructor are rated alike. The share of the unexplained variance that lies between instructors, the intraclass correlation of the residuals, is:

Code 
d$residual <- resid(m3)
ri <- nlme::lme(residual ~ 1, random = ~ 1 | prof, data = d)   # residuals: instructor part + course part
vc <- as.numeric(nlme::VarCorr(ri)[, "Variance"])
icc <- vc[1] / sum(vc)
avg_courses <- n / length(unique(d$prof))
c(icc = icc, courses_per_instructor = avg_courses, design_effect = 1 + (avg_courses - 1) * icc)
                   icc courses_per_instructor          design_effect 
             0.4029194              4.9255319              2.5816729

About 40% of what the model cannot explain is about who teaches the course. For a predictor that is constant within each instructor, like beauty, the 463 courses then carry about as much information as \(463 / \text{design effect} \approx\) 179 independent ones. Ordinary standard errors ignore this and are too small.

A quick fix is cluster-robust standard errors, which allow the residuals of the same instructor to be correlated:

Code 
vc_cl <- vcovCL(m3, cluster = ~ prof)       # courses clustered within instructors
coeftest(m3, vcov = vc_cl)

9. Reporting the results in APA style

A hierarchical regression report (APA 7th edition) gives the order of the blocks and why, R², \(\Delta R^2\) and the F-change of every step, and the coefficients of the final model. We collect the numbers from the R objects:

Code 
f2d  <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
nz   <- function(x, d = 2) sub("^(-?)0", "\\1", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))   # no leading zero
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", nz(p, 3))
s3   <- summary(m3)$coefficients
cl   <- coeftest(m3, vcov = vc_cl)

Method (data analysis):

Course evaluations were analysed with a three-step hierarchical regression. Instructor characteristics (gender, minority status, native English, age) were entered in Step 1, job and course characteristics (tenure track, lower division, single-credit course, class size as the base-2 logarithm of enrolment) in Step 2, and the instructor’s beauty rating in Step 3, so that beauty was credited only with variance not explained by the other predictors. Because the 463 courses were taught by 94 instructors, we also report standard errors clustered by instructor. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the sandwich and lmtest packages.

Results:

Instructor characteristics explained 5.3% of the variance in evaluations, R² = .05, F(4, 458) = 6.37, p < .001. Job and course characteristics explained an additional 7.4%, ΔR² = .07, F(4, 454) = 9.63, p < .001. Adding beauty in Step 3 increased the explained variance by a further 4.6%, ΔR² = .05, F(1, 453) = 25.10, p < .001, f² = .06. In the final model, R² = .17, adjusted R² = .16, more attractive instructors received higher evaluations, b = 0.16, SE = 0.03, β = .23, p < .001: one standard deviation of beauty was associated with 0.13 points higher evaluations on the 5-point scale. The effect remained significant with standard errors clustered by instructor, SE = 0.05, p = .001.
