thousands <- function(x) format(round(x, -3), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
more_or_fewer <- function(x) if (x >= 0) "more" else "fewer"
# the place of a country counted from the lowest: 1 is the lowest
lowest <- function(k) {
  if (k > 8) return(paste0("the ", k, "th lowest"))
  paste0("the ", c("", "second ", "third ", "fourth ", "fifth ", "sixth ", "seventh ", "eighth ")[k], "lowest")
}

1. How many people will Greece have?

Fewer every year: about 9.0 million in 2050 and 7.6 million in 2075, against 10.4 million today.

The population of Greece grew from 8.30 million in 1960 to 11.12 million in 2011. Since then it has fallen, to 10.37 million on 1 January 2026. In the baseline projection of Eurostat it keeps falling: to 8.96 million in 2050, 7.60 million in 2075 and 7.28 million in 2100, fewer than in 1960.

Code 
shown <- c(HMIGR = "dash", BSL = "solid", LFRT = "dot", NMIGR = "dashdot")
p <- plot_ly(history[!is.na(history$population), ],
  x = ~year, y = ~ population / 1e6, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Actual",
  line = list(color = "black", width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.2f} million<extra>Actual</extra>"
)
for (v in names(shown)) {
  projection <- future[future$projection == v, ]
  p <- add_trace(p,
    x = projection$year, y = projection$total / 1e6, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = variants[[v]],
    line = list(color = if (v == "BSL") greek_red else gray, width = if (v == "BSL") 3 else 2, dash = shown[[v]]),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.2f} million<extra>", variants[[v]], "</extra>"), inherit = FALSE
  )
}
in_2100 <- sapply(names(shown), function(v) ahead("total", 2100, v))
p %>% chart(
  "The population of Greece on 1 January, million", "Eurostat, demo_gind; projections: proj_23np (EUROPOP2023)", "Million",
  # a fixed range, or plotly widens the axis to fit the labels at the end of the lines
  x_axis = list(range = c(1958, 2102)),
  annotations = c(
    end_labels(2100, in_2100 / 1e6, paste0(variants[names(shown)], ": ", format(round(in_2100 / 1e6, 1), nsmall = 1))),
    list(list(x = peak_year, y = peak / 1e6, text = paste0(peak_year, ": the peak"), showarrow = TRUE, ax = 45, ay = -25))
  ),
  margin = list(t = 100, b = 90, r = 170), legend = legend_top
)

Interactive chart: The population of Greece on 1 January, million

The variants show what the result depends on. Migration matters most: with a third more migrants a year than in the baseline, Greece would have 8.3 million people in 2100; with no migration at all, 5.8 million. With a fifth fewer births, 6.3 million.

Code 
# the years since the start of the projection: what it assumed, and what happened
since <- 2023:last
assumed_over <- function(item) { x <- assumed(item); sum(x$values[x$time %in% since]) }
actual_over <- function(column) sum(history[[column]][history$year %in% since])
compare <- data.frame(
  item = c(paste("Births,", min(since), "to", last), paste("Deaths,", min(since), "to", last),
           paste("Net migration,", min(since), "to", last), paste("Population on 1 January", now)),
  projected = c(assumed_over("LBIRTH"), assumed_over("DEATH"), assumed_over("NMIGRAT"), ahead("total", now)),
  actual = c(actual_over("births"), actual_over("deaths"), actual_over("net_migration"), past("population", now))
)
compare$difference <- compare$actual - compare$projected
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  compare$item, format(compare$projected, big.mark = ","), format(compare$actual, big.mark = ","),
  paste0(ifelse(compare$difference > 0, "+", ""), format(compare$difference, big.mark = ","))
), col.names = c("", "Projected (baseline)", "Actual", "Difference"), align = "lrrr")
Projected (baseline) Actual Difference
Births, 2023 to 2025 232,127 204,997 -27,130
Deaths, 2023 to 2025 380,959 373,867 -7,092
Net migration, 2023 to 2025 -1,444 133,588 +135,032
Population on 1 January 2026 10,266,269 10,366,586 +100,317

Since 2022, the population has fallen more slowly than projected. On 1 January 2026, Greece had 100,000 more people than in the baseline. Births did not help: 27,000 fewer children were born from 2023 to 2025 than the projection assumed. Migration made the difference: in these years 134,000 more people came to Greece than left, while the projection assumed 1,000 more would leave than come. (Eurostat’s net migration of the past years includes a statistical adjustment.)

2. Why is the population falling?

Fewer children

Code 
tfr <- function(geo, year) fertility$values[fertility$geo == geo & fertility$time == year]
tfr_year <- max(fertility$time[fertility$geo == "EL"])
replacement_until <- max(fertility$time[fertility$geo == "EL" & fertility$values >= 2.1])
eu_tfr <- fertility[fertility$time == tfr_year & fertility$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ]

A population keeps its size without migration when each woman has about 2.1 children. Greek women had 2.23 children each in 1980, and fewer than 2.1 in every year since 1981. In 2024 they had 1.24, the seventh lowest in the EU, where the average was 1.34. Without migration, each generation would be about 59% as large as that of its parents.

Emigration in the crisis, immigration now

Code 
crisis <- history[history$year %in% 2010:2016, ]
migration_ahead <- assumed("NMIGRAT")
turns_positive <- min(migration_ahead$time[migration_ahead$time > last & migration_ahead$values > 0])
migration_in <- function(year) migration_ahead$values[migration_ahead$time == year]

In the crisis, more people left Greece than came: 278,000 more from 2010 to 2016. Since 2023 more come than leave, 50,000 more in 2025, but that does not make up for the gap between deaths and births, 55,000 in 2025. The baseline projection assumes that a few more people leave than come until 2033, and that from then on a few more come than leave: 8,000 in 2050 and 20,000 in 2070. In the chart, the blue bars are the years when more people came than left, the red bars the years when more left than came.

3. How old will it be?

Code 
aged_65 <- function(year) if (year <= ages_now) age_past("old", year) + age_past("oldest", year) else ahead("old", year) + ahead("oldest", year)
share_now <- 100 * aged_65(ages_now) / age_past("total")
share_2050 <- 100 * aged_65(2050) / ahead("total", 2050)
working_fall <- 100 * (1 - ahead("working", 2050) / age_past("working"))

Much older. In 2025, 24% of the people of Greece were 65 or over; in 2050, 35% will be. The number aged 80 and over grows from 0.74 million to 1.19 million, while the number aged 20 to 64, the age of almost all workers, falls by 29%, from 6.02 million to 4.29 million.

4. Who will work, and how much will they produce?

What an economy produces is the number of people who work, times what each of them produces. Greece has a problem with both.

Fewer workers

Code 
rate_now <- employed("EL")
rate_eu <- employed("EU27_2020")
rate_high <- 80
eu_rates <- employment[employment$geo %in% eu_countries$code & employment$age == "Y20-64" & employment$sex == "T" &
  employment$unit == "PC_POP" & employment$time == job_year, ]
jobs_now <- 1000 * employed("EL", unit = "THS_PER")
jobs_2013 <- 1000 * employed("EL", unit = "THS_PER", year = 2013)
women_gap <- employed("EU27_2020", sex = "F") - employed("EL", sex = "F")
men_gap <- employed("EU27_2020", sex = "M") - employed("EL", sex = "M")

Since 2013, the number of people aged 20 to 64 with a job in Greece has grown by 751,000, to 4.18 million, and the share of them who work, the employment rate, from 52.5% to 71.0%. That is how the economy recovered from the crisis. The rate is still the third lowest in the EU, where it is 76.1%, mainly because fewer women work: 62.3% of Greek women aged 20 to 64 have a job, against 71.3% in the EU, while for men the rates are 79.7% and 80.9%. Fewer older people work, too: 59.6% of those aged 55 to 64, against 66.4% in the EU.

With fewer people aged 20 to 64, the number of workers falls even if more of them work. The chart starts from the people with a job in 2025 and follows the people aged 20 to 64 of the baseline projection, at three employment rates, each reached in ten years:

Code 
# the employment rate of each year, from today's to the one of a scenario in ten years
rate_path <- function(years, to) rate_now + (to - rate_now) * pmin(1, pmax(0, (years - job_year) / 10))
years_ahead <- job_year:2075
workers_path <- function(to) {
  jobs_now * ahead("working", years_ahead) / ahead("working", job_year) * rate_path(years_ahead, to) / rate_now
}
paths <- data.frame(
  key = c("high", "eu", "stays"),
  rate = c(rate_high, rate_eu, rate_now),
  label = c(paste0("Reaches ", rate_high, "%"), paste0("Reaches the EU's ", percent(rate_eu)), paste0("Stays at ", percent(rate_now))),
  color = c(blue, greek_red, gray)
)
workers <- lapply(setNames(paths$rate, paths$key), workers_path)
jobs <- employment[employment$geo == "EL" & employment$age == "Y20-64" & employment$sex == "T" & employment$unit == "THS_PER", ]
p <- plot_ly(jobs,
  x = ~time, y = ~ values / 1000, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Actual",
  line = list(color = "black", width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.2f} million<extra>Actual</extra>"
)
for (k in seq_len(nrow(paths))) {
  p <- add_trace(p,
    x = years_ahead, y = workers[[paths$key[k]]] / 1e6, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = paths$label[k],
    line = list(color = paths$color[k], width = if (paths$key[k] == "eu") 3 else 2),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.2f} million<extra>", paths$label[k], "</extra>"), inherit = FALSE
  )
}
p %>% chart("People aged 20 to 64 in work, million, at three employment rates",
  "Eurostat, lfsi_emp_a and proj_23np (EUROPOP2023, baseline); own calculation", "Million",
  shapes = list(projection_start(job_year)), annotations = c(
    list(projection_label(job_year)),
    end_labels(2075, sapply(workers, function(w) w[length(w)]) / 1e6, percent(paths$rate))
  ),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90, r = 60), legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: People aged 20 to 64 in work, million, at three employment rates

Code 
fewer_in_2050 <- function(key) 100 * (1 - workers[[key]][years_ahead == 2050] / jobs_now)

If the employment rate stays at 71%, Greece has 28% fewer workers in 2050 than in 2025; at the EU’s 76%, 23% fewer. Even at 80%, a rate that 10 EU countries already have, it has 19% fewer.

Productivity that does not grow

Code 
productivity_year <- max(productivity$time)
since_2000 <- function(geo) productivity$index[productivity$geo == geo & productivity$time == productivity_year] - 100

What each worker produces has not grown in a quarter of a century. Output per person employed, after inflation, rose fast in Greece until 2008, fell in the crisis and is recovering, but in 2025 it was 4% lower than in 2000. In the EU it was 20% higher.

Code 
plot_ly(productivity[productivity$geo == "EL", ],
  x = ~time, y = ~index, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Greece",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}<extra>Greece</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = productivity[productivity$geo == "EU27_2020", ], x = ~time, y = ~index, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    name = "EU-27", line = list(color = blue, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}<extra>EU-27</extra>", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart("Output per person employed, after inflation, 2000 = 100", "Eurostat, nama_10_lp_ulc (real labour productivity per person)",
    "2000 = 100", legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: Output per person employed, after inflation, 2000 = 100

What it means for the economy

Code 
# GDP and the debt ratio year by year, from the last year of the debt to 2070. GDP grows with the
# number of people aged 20 to 64 who work and with what each of them produces (the people at work
# over 64 are left out); section 6 explains the debt.
debt_now <- debt("GD", "PC_GDP")
start_rate <- debt("D41PAY", "MIO_EUR") / debt("GD", "MIO_EUR", debt_year - 1)   # interest paid / debt a year earlier
rate_to <- 0.03       # the average interest rate on the debt in ten years
inflation <- 0.02     # a year
surplus <- 2.5        # the primary surplus, % of GDP
project <- function(productivity = 0.01, variant = "BSL", employment_to = rate_eu, shrink = TRUE, extra_pensions = FALSE) {
  years <- debt_year:2070
  people <- future[future$projection == variant, ]
  working <- people$working[match(years, people$year)]
  if (!shrink) working[] <- working[1]
  in_work <- working * rate_path(years, employment_to)
  real_growth <- in_work[-1] / in_work[-length(in_work)] * (1 + productivity) - 1
  growth <- (1 + real_growth) * (1 + inflation) - 1
  k <- seq_along(growth)
  interest <- start_rate + (rate_to - start_rate) * pmin(1, k / 10)
  primary <- rep(surplus, length(k))
  if (extra_pensions) primary <- primary - approx(constant_benefit$year, constant_benefit$extra, years[-1])$y
  ratio <- debt_now
  for (j in k) ratio[j + 1] <- ratio[j] * (1 + interest[j]) / (1 + growth[j]) - primary[j]
  gdp <- 100 * cumprod(c(1, 1 + real_growth))
  population <- people$total[match(years, people$year)]
  data.frame(year = years, gdp = gdp, gdp_person = gdp * population[1] / population, debt_gdp = ratio)
}
scenarios <- list(
  baseline = list(),
  no_fall = list(shrink = FALSE),
  fast = list(productivity = 0.016),
  flat = list(productivity = 0),
  more_migration = list(variant = "HMIGR"),
  no_migration = list(variant = "NMIGR"),
  rate_stays = list(employment_to = rate_now),
  rate_high = list(employment_to = rate_high),
  pensions = list(extra_pensions = TRUE)
)
scenario_names <- c(
  baseline = "Baseline: productivity +1% a year",
  no_fall = "The number of people aged 20 to 64 does not fall",
  fast = "Productivity +1.6% a year, as the Commission assumes",
  flat = "Productivity does not grow, as since 2000",
  more_migration = "Higher migration (EUROPOP2023 variant)",
  no_migration = "No migration (EUROPOP2023 variant)",
  rate_stays = paste("The employment rate stays at", percent(rate_now)),
  rate_high = paste0("The employment rate reaches ", rate_high, "%"),
  pensions = "Pensions keep their value against wages"
)
results <- lapply(scenarios, function(arguments) do.call(project, arguments))
at <- function(name, column, year) results[[name]][[column]][results[[name]]$year == year]
# the scenarios of the charts
lines <- data.frame(
  key = c("fast", "baseline", "flat", "no_fall"),
  label = c("Productivity +1.6% a year", "Productivity +1% a year", "Productivity flat", "+1%, with no fall in the people aged 20 to 64"),
  color = c(blue, greek_red, gray, dark_gray),
  dash = c("solid", "solid", "solid", "dash")
)
scenario_lines <- function(p, column, hover) {
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(lines))) {
    r <- results[[lines$key[k]]]
    p <- add_trace(p,
      x = r$year, y = r[[column]], type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = lines$label[k],
      line = list(color = lines$color[k], width = if (lines$key[k] == "baseline") 3 else 2, dash = lines$dash[k]),
      hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: ", hover, "<extra>", lines$label[k], "</extra>"), inherit = FALSE
    )
  }
  p
}
# the growth of productivity that keeps GDP as it is until 2050, at an employment rate, % a year
needed <- function(to) {
  ratio <- workers_path(to)[years_ahead == 2050] / jobs_now
  100 * (ratio^(-1 / (2050 - job_year)) - 1)
}

To keep the economy from shrinking, what each worker produces has to grow as fast as the number of workers falls: by 1.1% a year until 2050 if the employment rate reaches the EU’s, by 1.3% if it stays as it is. The European Commission assumes, in its Ageing Report, that productivity in Greece will grow by 1.6% a year until 2070, faster than in the EU (1.4%), while the hours worked fall by 0.6% a year, so that GDP grows by 1.1% a year, against 1.3% in the EU. All of Greece’s growth would come from productivity, growing for decades at a pace that it reached only in the years before 2008.

The chart follows GDP after inflation, with the employment rate reaching the EU’s in ten years, at three speeds of productivity; the dashed line shows what would happen if the number of people aged 20 to 64 did not fall:

Code 
scenario_lines(plot_ly(), "gdp", "%{y:.0f}") %>%
  chart(paste0("GDP after inflation, ", debt_year, " = 100"),
    "Eurostat, proj_23np (EUROPOP2023, baseline) and lfsi_emp_a; own scenarios", paste0(debt_year, " = 100"),
    legend = legend_top, margin = list(t = 100, b = 90))

Interactive chart: GDP after inflation, 2025 = 100

With productivity growing by 1% a year, GDP in 2050 is 99 (2025 = 100); if productivity does not grow, 77; at the 1.6% of the Commission, 114. Had the people aged 20 to 64 not been falling, the 1% would have taken it to 137.

A smaller economy is not necessarily a poorer one, as there are fewer people to share it: with productivity growing by 1% a year, GDP per person in 2050 is 14% higher than in 2025. But the debt does not shrink with the population, and the cost of an older population grows: both weigh more on a smaller economy.

5. What will pensions and health care cost?

Greece spends more on pensions than almost any EU country: 14.5% of GDP in 2022, against 11.4% in the EU. With many more older people for each person of working age, one would expect that to rise steeply. The Commission projects that it will not: 14.0% of GDP in 2050 and 12.0% in 2070, the largest fall in the EU.

Code 
reversed <- merge(constant_benefit, ageing[c("year", "pensions")])
plot_ly(ageing,
  x = ~year, y = ~pensions, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Greece",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 8),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Greece</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = reversed, x = ~year, y = ~ pensions + extra, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
    name = "Greece, if pensions keep their value against wages", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 2, dash = "dash"),
    marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 8, symbol = "circle-open"),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Pensions keep their value</extra>", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  add_trace(data = ageing, x = ~year, y = ~pensions_eu, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "EU",
    line = list(color = blue, width = 3), marker = list(color = blue, size = 8),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>EU</extra>", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart("Public spending on pensions, % of GDP, projected",
    "European Commission, 2024 Ageing Report, Table II.1.64; Greek pension fiche, Table 17", "% of GDP",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top)

Interactive chart: Public spending on pensions, % of GDP, projected

Why? The Greek pension fiche of the report breaks the change from 2022 to 2070 down (Table 8):

  • Ageing alone would add 7.7 points of GDP.
  • Smaller pensions against wages take 6.6 points off. Pensions rise with prices, while wages rise with prices and productivity, so the average pension falls from 76.4% of the average wage in 2022 to 57.1% in 2050 and 53.0% in 2070 (in the EU, from 43.2% to 35.8%).
  • More people in work take 2.2 points off.
  • Fewer people retiring early, as the retirement age follows life expectancy, take 0.7 points off.

These are the effects of the reforms of the 2010s. Their price is that each pensioner gets less against the wages of the time, and that is also their risk: if governments raise pensions with wages instead, to keep the benefit ratio of 2022, the report calculates that pensions would cost 2.8 points of GDP more in 2050 and 3.5 more in 2070 — more than the primary surplus assumed in the next section.

Health care costs more as people grow older, but the report expects only a small rise in Greece: from 5.4% of GDP in 2022 to 6.0% in 2050. Long-term care, for those who can no longer look after themselves, costs the Greek state almost nothing, 0.1% of GDP, against 1.7% in the EU, as families give most of it. With 1.19 million people aged 80 and over in 2050, against 0.74 million in 2025, and fewer children for each of them, that will be harder.

Altogether, the report puts what Greece spends on pensions, health care, long-term care and education at 23.4% of GDP in 2022 and 21.0% in 2070, while in the EU it rises from 24.4% to 25.6%. On paper, the cost of ageing is under control in Greece; in practice, that depends on pensions falling behind wages for decades.

6. What happens to the debt?

The debt ratio of next year is this year’s, grown by the interest rate and shrunk by the growth of GDP in euros, minus the primary surplus, the budget before interest:

\[d_{t} = d_{t-1} \times \frac{1 + i_t}{1 + g_t} - pb_t\]

The growth of GDP in euros is the growth of the number of workers, plus the growth of what each of them produces, plus inflation. A shrinking workforce takes something off it every year, so the debt shrinks more slowly against GDP.

The scenarios start from the debt of 2025, 145.4% of GDP, and assume, unless stated otherwise:

  • the people aged 20 to 64 of the baseline projection, of whom 71% work in 2025, rising to the EU’s 76% in ten years;
  • output per worker growing by 1% a year;
  • inflation of 2% a year, the target of the European Central Bank;
  • an average interest rate on the debt rising from 2.1% to 3% in ten years, as cheap loans are replaced by new borrowing at market rates;
  • a primary surplus of 2.5% of GDP every year, as in the steady scenario of the story on the Greek debt.

They are illustrations of how the population affects the debt, not forecasts.

Code 
actual <- edp[edp$na_item == "GD" & edp$unit == "PC_GDP" & edp$time >= 2010, ]
plot_ly(actual,
  x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Actual",
  line = list(color = "black", width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Actual</extra>"
) %>%
  scenario_lines("debt_gdp", "%{y:.0f}% of GDP") %>%
  chart("Greek government debt to 2070, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1, proj_23np and lfsi_emp_a; own scenarios",
    "% of GDP", y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top, margin = list(t = 120, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Greek government debt to 2070, % of GDP

The same scenarios and more, each changing one assumption of the baseline:

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  scenario_names[names(results)],
  sapply(names(results), function(s) round(at(s, "gdp", 2050))),
  sapply(names(results), function(s) percent(at(s, "debt_gdp", 2035))),
  sapply(names(results), function(s) percent(at(s, "debt_gdp", 2050))),
  sapply(names(results), function(s) percent(at(s, "debt_gdp", 2070)))
), col.names = c("Scenario", paste0("GDP in 2050 (", debt_year, " = 100)"), "Debt in 2035", "Debt in 2050", "Debt in 2070"),
row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
Scenario GDP in 2050 (2025 = 100) Debt in 2035 Debt in 2050 Debt in 2070
Baseline: productivity +1% a year 99 121% 108% 67%
The number of people aged 20 to 64 does not fall 137 106% 69% 19%
Productivity +1.6% a year, as the Commission assumes 114 113% 89% 37%
Productivity does not grow, as since 2000 77 135% 150% 143%
Higher migration (EUROPOP2023 variant) 104 118% 101% 55%
No migration (EUROPOP2023 variant) 100 118% 106% 72%
The employment rate stays at 71% 92 131% 120% 80%
The employment rate reaches 80% 104 114% 100% 58%
Pensions keep their value against wages 99 122% 134% 169%
Code 
debt_in <- function(name, year = 2050) round(at(name, "debt_gdp", year))
  • The shrinking population slows the fall of the debt. With productivity growing by 1% a year, the debt falls to 108% of GDP in 2050. If the people aged 20 to 64 did not fall, the same budget would bring it to 69%: the fall in the population costs about 39 points of GDP of debt by 2050.
  • Productivity decides. At 1.6% a year, as the Commission assumes, the debt is 89% of GDP in 2050. If productivity does not grow, as since 2000, it is 150% in 2050 and 143% in 2070: the debt stops falling, even with a primary surplus every year.
  • Migration helps, slowly: with the higher migration of the EUROPOP2023 variant, the debt is 101% of GDP in 2050 and 55% in 2070; with no migration at all, 106% and 72%. As the baseline assumes that a few more people leave than come until 2033, no migration at all does little harm at first.
  • So do more people in work: 100% if the employment rate reaches 80%, 120% if it stays at 71%.
  • Pensions are the largest risk of policy: if they keep their value against wages, and nothing else changes, the debt is 169% of GDP in 2070, instead of 67%.

So, what does it mean?

Greece will still be here in 2075, smaller and older: about 7.6 million people in the baseline projection, fewer than in 1960, and 33% of them aged 65 or over. A smaller population is not by itself a disaster: what matters for the economy and for the debt is how many people work, and what they produce.

  1. Productivity matters most. Output per worker has to grow by about 1.1% a year just to keep GDP from shrinking, and it has not grown since 2000. Between flat productivity and the 1.6% that the Commission assumes lie 61 points of GDP of debt in 2050.
  2. More people in work: fewer Greek women and fewer people over 55 work than in the rest of the EU, which leaves room to grow.
  3. Migration has already given Greece 100,000 more people than projected, and of all the variants of the projection it is the one that changes the population most.
  4. Pensions: the reforms keep the cost of ageing down by letting pensions fall behind wages. Undoing that would cost up to 4.0 points of GDP a year.
  5. Births take the longest: a child born today starts working in about twenty years, so more births would add workers only from the late 2040s.

The debt can keep falling while the population shrinks, but more slowly, and only if productivity grows: the one thing Greece has not managed since 2000.

Sources

  • Eurostat: proj_23np (population projections by age, EUROPOP2023), proj_23ndbi (projected births, deaths, migration and dependency), demo_gind (population, births, deaths and migration), demo_pjan (population by age), demo_pjanind (old-age dependency), demo_find (fertility), lfsi_emp_a (employment), nama_10_lp_ulc (productivity), gov_10dd_edpt1 (debt and interest).
  • European Commission: 2024 Ageing Report. Economic and Budgetary Projections for the EU Member States (2022-2070), Institutional Paper 279, April 2024 (Tables II.1.64, II.1.79, II.1.107, II.1.114, II.1.131 and II.1.135), and its pension fiche for Greece, prepared by the National Actuarial Authority (Tables 8 and 17).
  • European Commission: 2024 Ageing Report. Underlying Assumptions and Projection Methodologies, Institutional Paper 257, November 2023 (Tables I.3.1 to I.3.3: growth of GDP, hours worked and productivity).

See also

  • golemeurostat: a Shiny app for exploring the Eurostat indicators of the countries and regions of Europe (open the app)

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Greek Public Debt: How Much, to Whom, and Can Greece Repay It?
item.description: Greek public debt in Eurostat, World Bank and ESM data: how much Greece owes and to whom, how it compares with the economy and the EU, and whether it can repay.
item.content:encoded:
Greek public debt in Eurostat, World Bank and ESM data: how much Greece owes and to whom, how it compares with the economy and the EU, and whether it can repay.

What is this?

Greece went through one of the deepest debt crises of any modern European economy. More than fifteen years after the first bailout, this story answers four questions with official data:

  1. Does Greece owe more now than in 2010?
  2. Whom does it owe?
  3. How much is that compared with the size of the economy, and with the rest of the EU?
  4. Will Greece be able to repay?

The data come from three places:

  • Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU: the debt, the deficit, the interest, who holds the debt and when it falls due. They are downloaded when the page is rendered, so a new render brings in the latest figures.
  • The World Bank: interest payments as a share of the government’s revenue, back to 1972.
  • The Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) of Greece: who the creditors are, from its Annual Debt Bulletin 2025. The bulletin is a PDF, so its figures are typed in below, with the page they come from.

It follows two other stories of this site: Greece Since 2000 goes through the boom, the crisis and the recovery of the economy, and Same Crisis, Different Endings compares Greece with the other countries of the euro crisis; this one follows the debt.

Two measures of the same debt. Eurostat and the EU count the debt of the whole general government (the State, public bodies, local government and the pension funds) and leave out what one public body owes another: that is the figure of the EU rules, and of the headlines. The PDMA also reports the debt of the State alone, which includes the short-term loans that other public bodies make to the State with their spare cash. At the end of 2025 the first was €362.9 billion, the second €406.2 billion. This story uses the first, except where it names the creditors of the State.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
}
# debt, deficit and interest of the general government of Greece
edp <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list(
  geo = "EL", sector = "S13",
  na_item = c("GD", "GD_F3", "GD_F4", "B9", "D41PAY"),
  unit = c("MIO_EUR", "PC_GDP")
))
# gross domestic product at current prices, million euros
gdp <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(geo = "EL", na_item = "B1GQ", unit = "CP_MEUR"))
# one series of the deficit and debt data, by year
series <- function(item, unit, years) {
  s <- edp[edp$na_item == item & edp$unit == unit, ]
  s$values[match(years, s$time)]
}
years <- sort(unique(edp$time[edp$na_item == "GD"]))
greece <- data.frame(
  year = years,
  debt_bn = series("GD", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,          # debt, billion euros
  debt_gdp = series("GD", "PC_GDP", years),                 # debt, % of GDP
  bonds_bn = series("GD_F3", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,      # of which bonds and bills
  loans_bn = series("GD_F4", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,      # of which loans
  balance_gdp = series("B9", "PC_GDP", years),              # surplus (+) or deficit (-), % of GDP
  interest_gdp = series("D41PAY", "PC_GDP", years),         # interest, % of GDP
  interest_bn = series("D41PAY", "MIO_EUR", years) / 1000,
  gdp_bn = gdp$values[match(years, gdp$time)] / 1000
)
# the balance before interest: what the State collects minus what it spends on everything else
greece$primary_gdp <- greece$balance_gdp + greece$interest_gdp
last <- max(greece$year)
at <- function(column, year) greece[[column]][greece$year == year]
# who holds the debt (from 2020), and when it falls due
holders <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_ggd", list(geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", maturity = "TOTAL", unit = "MIO_EUR"))
due <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_rmd", list(geo = "EL", sector = "S13", na_item = "GD"))
# debt of every EU country, % of GDP, and the countries with the most
eu <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_edpt1", list(sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", unit = "PC_GDP"))
eu_name <- c(setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code), EU27_2020 = "EU-27")
most <- eu[eu$time == last & eu$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ]
most <- most[order(-most$values), ]
# the average years to repayment of the debt of every EU country, the longest first
maturities <- eurostat_values("gov_10dd_rmd", list(sector = "S13", na_item = "GD", maturity = "TOTAL", unit = "YR"))
maturities <- maturities[maturities$time == max(maturities$time) & maturities$geo %in% eu_countries$code, ]
maturities <- maturities[order(-maturities$values), ]
# World Bank: interest payments, % of revenue
world_bank <- jsonlite::fromJSON("https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/GRC/indicator/GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS?format=json&per_page=100")[[2]]
interest_revenue <- data.frame(year = as.integer(world_bank$date), value = world_bank$value)
interest_revenue <- interest_revenue[!is.na(interest_revenue$value), ]
interest_revenue <- interest_revenue[order(interest_revenue$year), ]
Code 
greek_red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left"),
    yaxis = list(title = y_title),
    xaxis = list(title = ""),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
# a short label of an amount
billion <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x), big.mark = ","), " bn")

1. Does Greece owe more now than in 2010?

In euros, yes. As a share of the economy, slightly less — and far less than at the peak.

At the end of 2010 the Greek state owed €331 bn; at the end of 2025 it owed €363 bn, that is €32 bn more. The debt fell only once, in 2012, when private holders of Greek bonds took a loss in the restructuring known as the PSI: between 2011 and 2012 the debt went down by €51 bn, although new bailout loans came in at the same time.

Code 
highlight <- ifelse(greece$year %in% c(2010, last), greek_red, gray)
plot_ly(greece,
  x = ~year, y = ~debt_bn, type = "bar", marker = list(color = highlight),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(
    "Greek government debt, billion euros", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "Billion euros",
    annotations = list(list(
      x = 2012, y = at("debt_bn", 2012), text = "2012: bondholders' haircut (PSI)",
      showarrow = TRUE, ax = 0, ay = -60
    ))
  )

Interactive chart: Greek government debt, billion euros

What matters for paying a debt is the size of the economy that carries it. As a share of the gross domestic product (GDP), the debt was 147.8% in 2010 and 145.4% in 2025: about the same. In between it rose to 209.4% in 2020, when the pandemic made the economy shrink, and it has fallen by 64 points since.

Code 
plot_ly(greece,
  x = ~year, y = ~debt_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_lines(x = range(greece$year), y = c(60, 60), line = list(color = gray, dash = "dash"), hoverinfo = "skip", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart(
    "Greek government debt, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "% of GDP",
    showlegend = FALSE,
    annotations = list(
      list(x = greece$year[1], y = 60, text = "60%: the limit of the EU rules", showarrow = FALSE, xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom", font = list(color = gray)),
      list(x = greece$year[which.max(greece$debt_gdp)], y = max(greece$debt_gdp), text = "Pandemic", showarrow = TRUE, ax = -50, ay = -30)
    )
  )

Interactive chart: Greek government debt, % of GDP

2. Whom does Greece owe?

Mostly the rest of the euro area, through the rescue funds of the bailouts. In 2010, 79% of the debt was bonds sold to investors; in 2025, 71% is loans. The bailouts replaced most of the bonds with long, cheap loans from the euro area and, until 2022, the IMF.

Code 
plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~bonds_bn, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Bonds and bills",
  line = list(color = gray, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion in bonds<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~loans_bn, name = "Loans", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion in loans<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("From bonds to loans: the debt by instrument, billion euros", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1", "Billion euros",
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))

Interactive chart: From bonds to loans: the debt by instrument, billion euros

The PDMA names the creditors of the State. At the end of 2025:

Code 
# PDMA, Annual Debt Bulletin 2025 (June 2026), debt of the State at 31.12.2025, million euros (pages 13-14).
# The bulletin gives 211,421 for the loans of the EFSF, the ESM and the GLF together, and says
# that the EFSF and the ESM hold 45.58% of the debt; the GLF is the difference.
total <- 406181
creditors <- data.frame(
  creditor = c(
    "EFSF and ESM: the euro area rescue funds",
    "Bonds held by investors and the Bank of Greece",
    "Repos: short-term loans, mostly from public bodies",
    "GLF: bilateral loans of euro area countries",
    "Other EU and international loans (RRF, SURE, EIB)",
    "Treasury bills"
  ),
  million = c(round(0.4558 * total), 100759, 62852, 211421 - round(0.4558 * total), 23057, 7969)
)
creditors$share <- 100 * creditors$million / total
creditors <- creditors[order(creditors$million), ]
creditors$creditor <- factor(creditors$creditor, levels = creditors$creditor)
plot_ly(creditors,
  x = ~ million / 1000, y = ~creditor, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = c(rep(gray, nrow(creditors) - 1), greek_red)),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share, 1), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: €%{x:.1f} billion<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Who lends to the Greek State, end of 2025, billion euros",
    "PDMA, Annual Debt Bulletin 2025; the GLF as calculated in the code above",
    margin = list(l = 330, r = 60, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Who lends to the Greek State, end of 2025, billion euros

  • The EFSF and the ESM, the rescue funds of the euro area, hold almost half of the debt of the State. Their loans are repaid over decades: those of the EFSF from 2023 to 2070, those of the ESM from 2034 to 2060 (ESM).
  • The GLF loans of the first bailout come from the other euro area countries. Their interest rate floats, so Greece is paying them back early: €5.3 billion in 2025.
  • The IMF was repaid in full in 2022.
  • The repos are mostly the cash of other public bodies, lent to the State for a few days or weeks; the EU measure of the debt leaves them out.

Eurostat’s view of the same debt, by who holds it rather than by instrument:

Code 
groups <- c(
  S2 = "Abroad (the rescue funds, foreign investors)",
  S121 = "Bank of Greece",
  S122_S123 = "Greek banks",
  `S124-S129` = "Other Greek financial companies",
  S11 = "Greek companies",
  S14_S15 = "Greek households"
)
latest_holders <- holders[holders$time == max(holders$time), ]
held <- data.frame(holder = groups, million = latest_holders$values[match(names(groups), latest_holders$sector2)])
held$million[is.na(held$million)] <- 0
held$share <- 100 * held$million / latest_holders$values[latest_holders$sector2 == "S1_S2"]
held <- held[order(held$share), ]
held$holder <- factor(held$holder, levels = held$holder)
plot_ly(held,
  x = ~share, y = ~holder, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(held$holder == groups[["S2"]], greek_red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of the debt<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Who holds the Greek government debt, ", max(holders$time), ", % of the debt"),
    "Eurostat, gov_10dd_ggd", margin = list(l = 300, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Who holds the Greek government debt, 2025, % of the debt

3. How much is it, compared with the economy and with the EU?

At 145.4% of GDP, Greece still has the highest debt in the EU, 8.7 points above Italy.

Code 
eu_latest <- eu[eu$time == last & eu$geo %in% c(eu_countries$code, "EU27_2020"), ]
eu_latest$name <- eu_name[eu_latest$geo]
eu_latest <- eu_latest[order(eu_latest$values), ]
eu_latest$name <- factor(eu_latest$name, levels = eu_latest$name)
plot_ly(eu_latest,
  x = ~values, y = ~name, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(eu_latest$geo == "EL", greek_red, ifelse(eu_latest$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))),
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Government debt in the EU, ", last, ", % of GDP"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1",
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90))

Interactive chart: Government debt in the EU, 2025, % of GDP

4. Will Greece be able to repay?

Countries rarely pay their debt off; they repay old loans with new ones. The question is whether the debt stays affordable — whether the interest leaves enough for everything else — and whether it keeps shrinking against the economy. On both, the numbers now look good, for four reasons.

Interest takes far less of the budget

In 2011 interest cost Greece 7.7% of GDP; in 2025, 3.1%. The World Bank’s series shows the same from the side of the budget: interest took 17.8% of the government’s revenue in 2011, and 7.5% in 2024.

Code 
subplot(
  plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~interest_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3),
    name = "% of GDP (Eurostat)", hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"),
  plot_ly(interest_revenue, x = ~year, y = ~value, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", line = list(color = blue, width = 3),
    name = "% of revenue (World Bank)", hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of revenue<extra></extra>"),
  nrows = 2, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE
) %>%
  chart("Interest paid by the Greek government", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1; World Bank, GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS",
    "% of GDP", yaxis2 = list(title = "% of revenue"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))

Interactive chart: Interest paid by the Greek government

The debt is long, fixed and in euros

Code 
years_left <- due[due$unit == "YR" & due$maturity == "TOTAL", ]
buckets <- c(Y_LE1 = "Up to 1 year", `Y1-5` = "1 to 5 years", `Y5-10` = "5 to 10 years", `Y10-30` = "10 to 30 years", Y_GT30 = "Over 30 years")
falling_due <- due[due$unit == "MIO_EUR" & due$time == max(due$time) & due$maturity %in% names(buckets), ]
falling_due$label <- factor(buckets[falling_due$maturity], levels = buckets)
falling_due$share <- 100 * falling_due$values / sum(falling_due$values)
plot_ly(falling_due,
  x = ~label, y = ~share, type = "bar", marker = list(color = greek_red),
  text = ~ paste0(round(share), "%"), textposition = "outside", cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of the debt<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("When the debt falls due, ", max(due$time), ", % of the debt"), "Eurostat, gov_10dd_rmd", "% of the debt")

Interactive chart: When the debt falls due, 2025, % of the debt

  • On average the debt falls due in 18.4 years (Eurostat), the longest in the EU: next comes Austria, with 11.3 years.
  • After interest rate swaps, none of it has a floating rate and none is in a foreign currency (PDMA): higher interest rates reach only the debt that is renewed, a little each year.
  • In 2025 the State needed €17.6 billion to repay maturing debt and cover its budget, about 7% of GDP, and borrowed it at 2.89% for 14.6 years on average (PDMA). When the euro area eased the terms of its loans in 2018, it set out to keep these needs below 15% of GDP in the medium term and below 20% after that (Eurogroup, June 2018).
  • The State keeps a cash reserve: the general government held €39.6 billion in cash at the end of 2025, so its debt minus its cash was €323 billion (PDMA).

Why the ratio fell so fast

The change of the debt ratio each year adds up from four parts:

  • Interest adds to the debt.
  • The primary balance (the budget before interest) adds a deficit or takes away a surplus.
  • Growth of the economy in euros — real growth plus inflation — shrinks the ratio, as the same debt is divided by a bigger GDP.
  • Other changes: debt that changes without a deficit, such as the PSI haircut of 2012 or the cash the State borrows ahead and keeps.
Code 
d <- greece[greece$year >= 2010 & !is.na(greece$gdp_bn), ]
n <- nrow(d)
ratio <- 100 * d$debt_bn / d$gdp_bn
growth <- d$gdp_bn[-1] / d$gdp_bn[-n] - 1
parts <- data.frame(
  year = d$year[-1],
  change = diff(ratio),
  interest = 100 * d$interest_bn[-1] / d$gdp_bn[-1],
  primary = -d$primary_gdp[-1],
  growth = -ratio[-n] * growth / (1 + growth)
)
parts$other <- parts$change - parts$interest - parts$primary - parts$growth
plot_ly(parts, x = ~year, y = ~interest, type = "bar", name = "Interest", marker = list(color = greek_red)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~primary, name = "Primary deficit (+) or surplus (-)", marker = list(color = "#ff9896")) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~growth, name = "Growth of GDP in euros", marker = list(color = blue)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~other, name = "Other", marker = list(color = gray)) %>%
  add_trace(y = ~change, type = "scatter", mode = "markers", name = "Change of the debt ratio",
    marker = list(color = "black", size = 10, symbol = "diamond")) %>%
  chart("What changed the debt ratio each year, points of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1 and nama_10_gdp; own calculation",
    "Points of GDP", barmode = "relative", note_y = -0.34, margin = list(t = 70, b = 160),
    # under the chart, as its five entries take two lines
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.1, yanchor = "top"))

Interactive chart: What changed the debt ratio each year, points of GDP

From 2021 the economy grew fast in euros — partly real growth, partly inflation — while the interest rate on the debt stayed low: growth alone took 71 points off the ratio between 2021 and 2025. The budget before interest was in deficit in the pandemic and then turned to surplus: from 2023, the surpluses took 12 points more.

Where it could go: three scenarios

The debt ratio of next year is this year’s, grown by the interest rate and shrunk by the growth of GDP in euros, minus the primary surplus:

\[d_{t} = d_{t-1} \times \frac{1 + i_t}{1 + g_t} - pb_t\]

The scenarios below start from the 2025 debt and its average interest rate of 2.1%, which climbs over ten years as cheap loans are replaced by new borrowing at market rates. They are illustrations of what drives the debt, not forecasts.

Code 
start_rate <- at("interest_bn", last) / at("debt_bn", last - 1)
assumptions <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("Strong", "Steady", "Weak"),
  growth = c(0.050, 0.040, 0.025),    # growth of GDP in euros, a year
  rate_to = c(0.025, 0.030, 0.040),   # average interest rate on the debt after ten years
  primary = c(3.5, 2.5, 1.0)          # primary surplus, % of GDP
)
project <- function(growth, rate_to, primary, years = (last + 1):2040) {
  debt <- at("debt_gdp", last)
  path <- numeric(length(years))
  for (k in seq_along(years)) {
    rate <- start_rate + (rate_to - start_rate) * min(1, k / 10)
    debt <- debt * (1 + rate) / (1 + growth) - primary
    path[k] <- debt
  }
  data.frame(year = c(last, years), debt_gdp = c(at("debt_gdp", last), path))
}
paths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(assumptions)), function(k) {
  cbind(scenario = assumptions$scenario[k], project(assumptions$growth[k], assumptions$rate_to[k], assumptions$primary[k]))
}))
in_2040 <- setNames(paths$debt_gdp[paths$year == 2040], paths$scenario[paths$year == 2040])
knitr::kable(transform(assumptions,
  growth = paste0(100 * growth, "%"), rate_to = paste0(100 * rate_to, "%"), primary = paste0(primary, "% of GDP"),
  debt_2040 = paste0(round(in_2040[scenario]), "% of GDP")
), col.names = c("Scenario", "GDP growth in euros, a year", "Interest rate after ten years", "Primary surplus", "Debt in 2040"))
Scenario GDP growth in euros, a year Interest rate after ten years Primary surplus Debt in 2040
Strong 5% 2.5% 3.5% of GDP 55% of GDP
Steady 4% 3% 2.5% of GDP 86% of GDP
Weak 2.5% 4% 1% of GDP 150% of GDP
Code 
plot_ly(greece, x = ~year, y = ~debt_gdp, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Actual",
  line = list(color = "black", width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Strong", ], name = "Strong", line = list(color = blue, dash = "dot")) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Steady", ], name = "Steady", line = list(color = greek_red, dash = "dot")) %>%
  add_trace(data = paths[paths$scenario == "Weak", ], name = "Weak", line = list(color = gray, dash = "dot")) %>%
  chart("Greek government debt to 2040: three scenarios, % of GDP", "Eurostat, gov_10dd_edpt1; own scenarios", "% of GDP",
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"))

Interactive chart: Greek government debt to 2040: three scenarios, % of GDP

In the steady scenario the debt falls to about 86% of GDP by 2040. In the weak one it ends near 150%, a little above today’s level: with long, fixed and cheap loans, a bad decade would stop the fall rather than send the debt back to the heights of 2020.

So, will Greece repay?

On today’s numbers, yes: the debt is large, but it is cheap, it falls due slowly, and it is shrinking against the economy. The markets agree: Greece is back in the investment grade (Moody’s raised it to Baa3 in March 2025), and at the end of 2025 its ten-year bonds paid only 0.59 percentage points more than Germany’s (PDMA).

What could still go wrong:

  • A recession, or years of slow growth: growth did most of the work since 2021.
  • Higher interest rates on the debt that is renewed each year, and more of it once the cheap rescue loans start falling due in the 2030s.
  • Smaller surpluses: the scenarios need primary surpluses for many years, which is a political choice, not only an economic one.
  • An ageing population, which raises the cost of pensions and health care.

Sources

  • Eurostat: gov_10dd_edpt1 (deficit, debt and interest), gov_10dd_ggd (holders of the debt), gov_10dd_rmd (remaining maturity), nama_10_gdp (GDP).
  • World Bank: Interest payments (% of revenue), GC.XPN.INTP.RV.ZS.
  • PDMA, Ministry of Finance: Annual Debt Bulletin 2025 (in Greek, June 2026).
  • ESM: When will Greece repay ESM and EFSF loans?

See also

  • golemeurostat: a Shiny app for exploring the Eurostat indicators of the countries and regions of Europe (open the app)
  • golemworldbank: an interactive explorer of the World Bank development indicators of every country (open the app)

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Tobit Regression: A Worked Example
item.description: Tobit regression for an outcome censored at zero, fitted in R with AER and censReg on simulated data, explained step by step and reported in APA style.
item.content:encoded:
Tobit regression for an outcome censored at zero, fitted in R with AER and censReg on simulated data, explained step by step and reported in APA style.

The problem: a pile of zeros

Imagine we ask 500 people how many hours per week they spend on sport. Many answer 0. Not because they all have exactly the same “zero” interest in sport: some are almost ready to start, others would never do it. We only see 0, because hours cannot go below 0.

This is called a censored outcome: below a limit (here 0) we do not see the true value, only the limit itself.

A Tobit model assumes there is an unobserved (latent) variable \(y^*\), the person’s “desire” for sport, that follows an ordinary linear regression:

\[y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]

and what we observe is

\[y = \begin{cases} y^* & \text{if } y^* > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } y^* \le 0 \end{cases}\]

To see why we need it, we simulate data where we know the true answer, and compare three methods.

Code 
library(survival)   # survreg(): fits the Tobit model (comes with R)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)  # put plots side by side

1. Simulate the data

The true model: every extra hour of free time per day adds 2 hours of sport per week (\(\beta_1 = 2\)), starting from \(-4\) (\(\beta_0 = -4\)), with noise \(\sigma = 3\).

Code 
set.seed(42)
n <- 500
free_time <- runif(n, 0, 6)                         # hours of free time per day
latent    <- -4 + 2 * free_time + rnorm(n, sd = 3)  # y*: the true "desire" (can be negative)
hours     <- pmax(latent, 0)                        # y: what we observe (never below 0)
df <- data.frame(free_time, latent, hours, censored = latent <= 0)
mean(df$censored)   # share of people we see as 0
[1] 0.362

About a third of the people are recorded as exactly 0.

2. Look at the data

Code 
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#0082c8", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "What we observe", x = "hours of sport per week", y = "people")
p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(latent, fill = censored)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#0082c8", `TRUE` = "#E74C3C"),
                    labels = c("observed", "hidden: recorded as 0")) +
  labs(title = "The truth (never seen in real life)", x = "latent y*", y = "people", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p1 + p2

Left: the big bar at 0 is the pile-up. Right: behind that bar are many different negative values (red), all squeezed into a single 0.

Code 
ggplot(df, aes(free_time)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = latent), colour = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.35, size = 1.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = hours), colour = "#0082c8", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "Red: the true y*.  Blue: what we observe (red points below 0 are moved up to 0)",
       x = "free time (hours per day)", y = "hours of sport")

3. Three ways to fit it

Code 
ols_all  <- lm(hours ~ free_time, data = df)                    # (a) ignore the problem
ols_pos  <- lm(hours ~ free_time, data = subset(df, hours > 0)) # (b) drop the zeros
tobit    <- survreg(Surv(hours, hours > 0, type = "left") ~ free_time,
                    data = df, dist = "gaussian")               # (c) Tobit
summary(tobit)

Call:
survreg(formula = Surv(hours, hours > 0, type = "left") ~ free_time, 
    data = df, dist = "gaussian")
              Value Std. Error     z      p
(Intercept) -4.0633     0.3514 -11.6 <2e-16
free_time    1.9795     0.0923  21.4 <2e-16
Log(scale)   1.0818     0.0410  26.4 <2e-16
Scale= 2.95 
Gaussian distribution
Loglik(model)= -896.3   Loglik(intercept only)= -1095.5
    Chisq= 398.29 on 1 degrees of freedom, p= 1.3e-88 
Number of Newton-Raphson Iterations: 6 
n= 500

Surv(hours, hours > 0, type = "left") tells R: “hours is the value, it is a real observation when hours > 0, and otherwise it is left-censored (the true value is somewhere at or below 0).” With dist = "gaussian" this is exactly the Tobit model. (AER::tobit(hours ~ free_time, left = 0) gives the same result with a shorter call.)

How to read the output

The output of summary(tobit) above, part by part. The coefficient table is also available as numbers, which we use below:

Code 
s <- summary(tobit)$table   # Value, Std. Error, z, p for each row
signif(s, 4)                # signif, not round: round() would print the tiny p values as 0
             Value Std. Error      z          p
(Intercept) -4.063    0.35140 -11.56  6.249e-31
free_time    1.980    0.09227  21.45 4.135e-102
Log(scale)   1.082    0.04101  26.38 2.418e-153

The coefficient table. Each row is one parameter:

Column Meaning Here, for free_time
Value The estimate \(b\): the change in the latent \(y^*\) for one unit more of the predictor 1.98: one more hour of free time per day raises the latent amount of sport by about 2 hours per week
Std. Error How uncertain the estimate is; smaller is more precise 0.09
z Value / Std. Error: how many standard errors the estimate is away from 0 1.9795 / 0.0923 = 21.45
p The chance of a z this large if the true effect were 0. <2e-16 means smaller than 0.0000000000000002: report it as p < .001 <2e-16
  • (Intercept) (-4.06) is the predicted latent value for someone with 0 hours of free time. It is below 0, which means such a person is predicted to do no sport at all. It is not a prediction of observed hours, which can never be negative.
  • Log(scale) is the logarithm of \(\sigma\), the standard deviation of the errors. Its z and p test whether \(\sigma = 1\), which is not an interesting question: ignore them.
  • Scale= is \(\sigma\) itself (2.95; the true value in our simulation is 3). It is the spread of \(y^*\) around the regression line, and it is needed for the formulas in section 4.
  • Gaussian distribution confirms that the errors are assumed normal, which is what makes this a Tobit model.
  • Loglik(model) and Loglik(intercept only) measure how well the model with and without free_time fits the data (higher, i.e. closer to 0, is better).
  • Chisq= ... on 1 degrees of freedom, p= ... is the likelihood-ratio test: twice the difference of the two log-likelihoods, \(2 \times (-896.3 - (-1095.5)) = 398.29\). It tests whether the predictors together improve the model; the degrees of freedom are the number of predictors.
  • Number of Newton-Raphson Iterations is technical: the estimation converged after that many steps. If R warns that it did not converge, do not trust the results.
  • n= counts all participants, the censored ones too: Tobit uses them, which is the whole point.

Two things are not in the output. There is no \(R^2\): Tobit is fitted by maximum likelihood, so use the likelihood-ratio test to judge the model. And the coefficients are effects on the latent \(y^*\), not on the observed hours; for those, see sections 4 and 5.

Code 
data.frame(
  method    = c("Truth", "(a) OLS, all data", "(b) OLS, zeros dropped", "(c) Tobit"),
  intercept = round(c(-4, coef(ols_all)[1], coef(ols_pos)[1], coef(tobit)[1]), 2),
  slope     = round(c( 2, coef(ols_all)[2], coef(ols_pos)[2], coef(tobit)[2]), 2)
)
                  method intercept slope
1                  Truth     -4.00  2.00
2      (a) OLS, all data     -1.09  1.34
3 (b) OLS, zeros dropped     -0.28  1.26
4              (c) Tobit     -4.06  1.98
Code 
grid <- data.frame(free_time = seq(0, 6, length.out = 100))
lines <- rbind(
  data.frame(grid, y = -4 + 2 * grid$free_time,         method = "Truth"),
  data.frame(grid, y = predict(ols_all, grid),          method = "(a) OLS, all data"),
  data.frame(grid, y = predict(ols_pos, grid),          method = "(b) OLS, zeros dropped"),
  data.frame(grid, y = predict(tobit, grid),            method = "(c) Tobit")
)
ggplot(df, aes(free_time, hours)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = lines, aes(y = y, colour = method, linetype = method), linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Truth" = "black", "(a) OLS, all data" = "#E74C3C",
                                 "(b) OLS, zeros dropped" = "#f39c12", "(c) Tobit" = "#0082c8")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Truth" = "dashed", "(a) OLS, all data" = "solid",
                                   "(b) OLS, zeros dropped" = "solid", "(c) Tobit" = "solid")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Only Tobit recovers the true line", x = "free time (hours per day)",
       y = "hours of sport", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
  • (a) OLS on all data is too flat: the zeros pull the left end of the line up, so the effect of free time looks smaller than it is.
  • (b) OLS without the zeros is also too flat: we kept only people whose noise happened to be high enough, so the sample is no longer random.
  • (c) Tobit lands on the true line, because it uses the zeros correctly: as “somewhere at or below 0”, not as “exactly 0”.

4. The model step by step, with formulas

Two functions of the normal (bell) curve appear in every formula below:

  • \(\phi(z)\) (“small phi”) is the height of the standard normal curve at \(z\). In R: dnorm(z).
  • \(\Phi(z)\) (“capital phi”) is the area under the curve to the left of \(z\): the share of a normal population that lies below \(z\) standard deviations. In R: pnorm(z). For example \(\Phi(0) = 0.5\) and \(\Phi(1.96) = 0.975\).

Step 1: a straight line (yes, \(y = ax + b\))

At its heart, the Tobit model is the straight line from school, \(y = ax + b\). Statistics books write it as

\[y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]

  • \(\beta_1\) is the \(a\): the slope, how much the line goes up for one unit more of \(x\).
  • \(\beta_0\) is the \(b\): the intercept, the height of the line at \(x = 0\).
Code 
b0 <- unname(coef(tobit)["(Intercept)"])   # the "b" of y = ax + b
b1 <- unname(coef(tobit)["free_time"])     # the "a": the slope
sigma <- tobit$scale
x0 <- 3                                     # a person with 3 hours of free time per day
line0 <- b0 + b1 * x0
line0
[1] 1.875369

For a person with \(x = 3\) hours of free time:

\[y^* = -4.06 + 1.98 \times 3 = 1.88\]

What makes Tobit different from ordinary regression is steps 2 and 3.

Step 2: people are scattered around the line

\[y^* = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\]

Two people with the same free time do not want the same amount of sport. \(\varepsilon\) (“epsilon”) is how far each person is from the line. It is normally distributed around 0 with standard deviation \(\sigma\) = 2.95, so about two thirds of the people are within \(\pm\) 2.95 hours of the line, and about 95% within \(\pm 2\sigma\).

Step 3: the floor at 0

\[y = \max(0,\; y^*)\]

We see \(y^*\) only when it is positive. Everyone whose \(y^*\) falls at or below 0 is recorded as exactly 0.

Step 4: the chance of being at 0

For a person with free time \(x\), the line is at \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) and \(y^*\) is spread around it with standard deviation \(\sigma\). The chance of falling at or below 0 is the area of that bell curve below 0:

\[P(y = 0 \mid x) = P(y^* \le 0) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{0 - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x)}{\sigma}\right)\]

In words: how many standard deviations is 0 below the line, and what share of the bell curve lies below that point? Writing \(z = \frac{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}{\sigma}\) for the height of the line in standard deviations, this is \(\Phi(-z)\), and the chance of doing some sport is \(P(y > 0 \mid x) = \Phi(z)\).

Code 
z0 <- line0 / sigma                 # the line at x = 3, in standard deviations
p_zero <- pnorm(-z0)                # Φ(-z): the area of the bell curve below 0
c(z = z0, chance_of_zero = p_zero)
             z chance_of_zero 
     0.6357350      0.2624746
Code 
near <- abs(df$free_time - x0) < 0.5       # people in the data with 2.5 to 3.5 hours
mean(df$hours[near] == 0)                   # the share of them who are at 0: close to the formula
[1] 0.2282609

For \(x = 3\): \(z = 1.88 / 2.95 = 0.64\), so \(P(y = 0) = \Phi(-0.64) = 0.26\): about 26% of such people do no sport.

Code 
dens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(1, 3, 5), function(x) {
  mu <- b0 + b1 * x
  y <- seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 400)
  data.frame(y = y, d = dnorm(y, mu, sigma),
             label = sprintf("free time = %d hour%s: line at %.2f, P(y = 0) = %.2f",
                             x, ifelse(x == 1, "", "s"), mu, pnorm(-mu / sigma)))
}))
ggplot(dens, aes(y, d)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(dens, y <= 0), fill = "#E74C3C", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~label, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Where y* can fall for three people. The red area is recorded as 0",
       x = "latent y* (hours of sport per week)", y = "density")

The more free time, the further the bell curve moves to the right, and the smaller the red area.

Step 5: how R finds \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma\)

R uses maximum likelihood: it looks for the values that make the data we saw as likely as possible. Every person adds one piece:

  • A person with \(y_i > 0\): we know the exact value, so the piece is the height of their bell curve at that value: \(\frac{1}{\sigma}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)}{\sigma}\right)\), in R dnorm(y, mean = line, sd = sigma).
  • A person with \(y_i = 0\): we only know that \(y^* \le 0\), so the piece is the red area of their bell curve: \(\Phi\!\left(\frac{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i)}{\sigma}\right)\), in R pnorm(-line / sigma).

Adding the logarithms of all the pieces gives the log-likelihood:

\[\log L = \sum_{y_i > 0} \log\!\left[\frac{1}{\sigma}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i}{\sigma}\right)\right] + \sum_{y_i = 0} \log \Phi\!\left(\frac{-\beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i}{\sigma}\right)\]

R tries values of \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) and \(\sigma\) until \(\log L\) is as large as possible. With the estimates, our hand calculation gives exactly the Loglik(model) of the output:

Code 
line_i <- b0 + b1 * df$free_time      # the line for every person
pos    <- df$hours > 0
loglik_by_hand <- sum(log(dnorm(df$hours[pos], mean = line_i[pos], sd = sigma))) +   # people above 0: heights
                  sum(log(pnorm(-line_i[!pos] / sigma)))                             # people at 0: areas
c(by_hand = loglik_by_hand, from_R = tobit$loglik[2])
  by_hand    from_R 
-896.3469 -896.3469

Ordinary regression (OLS) instead treats every 0 as an exact value of 0, the first kind of piece, which is why its line comes out too flat.

Step 6: three different “averages”

For people with free time \(x\), with \(z = \frac{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}{\sigma}\) as before, there are three different average amounts of sport:

  1. The line, the average of \(y^*\) (it can be negative): \(E[y^* \mid x] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)
  2. Among the people who do some sport: \(E[y \mid y > 0, x] = (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) + \sigma \, \dfrac{\phi(z)}{\Phi(z)}\). It is above the line, because the people with the lowest \(y^*\) have dropped out to 0.
  3. Among everybody, zeros included: \(E[y \mid x] = \Phi(z)\,(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) + \sigma\,\phi(z)\). This is the chance of doing any sport times the average of those who do: \(P(y > 0) \times E[y \mid y > 0]\).
Code 
e_line      <- line0
e_positive  <- line0 + sigma * dnorm(z0) / pnorm(z0)
e_everybody <- pnorm(z0) * line0 + sigma * dnorm(z0)
round(c(line = e_line, among_those_doing_sport = e_positive, everybody = e_everybody), 2)
                   line among_those_doing_sport               everybody 
                   1.88                    3.18                    2.34
Code 
# the same in the data, for people with 2.5 to 3.5 hours of free time
round(c(among_those_doing_sport = mean(df$hours[near & df$hours > 0]), everybody = mean(df$hours[near])), 2)
among_those_doing_sport               everybody 
                   3.05                    2.36
Code 
x  <- seq(0, 6, length.out = 200)
zx <- (b0 + b1 * x) / sigma
curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(free_time = x, y = b0 + b1 * x, what = "1. the line, E[y*]"),
  data.frame(free_time = x, y = b0 + b1 * x + sigma * dnorm(zx) / pnorm(zx), what = "2. those doing sport, E[y | y > 0]"),
  data.frame(free_time = x, y = pnorm(zx) * (b0 + b1 * x) + sigma * dnorm(zx), what = "3. everybody, E[y]"))
ggplot(df, aes(free_time, hours)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = curves, aes(y = y, colour = what, linetype = what), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", "#f39c12", "#0082c8")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("dashed", "solid", "solid")) +
  labs(title = "Three averages: they come together when almost nobody is at 0",
       x = "free time (hours per day)", y = "hours of sport per week", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Step 7: the effect of one more unit of \(x\)

The effect is the slope of each “average” from step 6:

  • On the latent \(y^*\), the slope of the straight line: \(\dfrac{\partial E[y^*]}{\partial x} = \beta_1\)
  • On the observed hours, the slope times the chance of being above 0: \(\dfrac{\partial E[y \mid x]}{\partial x} = \beta_1\,\Phi(z)\)
  • On the chance of doing any sport: \(\dfrac{\partial P(y > 0 \mid x)}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\beta_1}{\sigma}\,\phi(z)\)

The average marginal effect is the second one, averaged over all \(n\) people: \(\text{AME} = \beta_1 \cdot \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \Phi(z_i)\).

Code 
me_line  <- b1                                   # effect on y*
me_hours <- b1 * pnorm(z0)                       # effect on the observed hours, at x = 3
me_prob  <- b1 / sigma * dnorm(z0)               # effect on the chance of doing any sport, at x = 3
ame_hand <- b1 * mean(pnorm(line_i / sigma))     # effect on the observed hours, averaged over everybody
round(c(on_y_star = me_line, on_hours_at_3 = me_hours, on_chance_at_3 = me_prob, average_on_hours = ame_hand), 3)
       on_y_star    on_hours_at_3   on_chance_at_3 average_on_hours 
           1.980            1.460            0.219            1.257

For a person with 3 hours of free time, one more hour adds \(1.98 \times 0.74 = 1.46\) hours of sport and raises the chance of doing any sport by about 22 percentage points. Averaged over everybody, it adds 1.26 hours: the same number as in section 5.

All the formulas at once

Quantity Formula R
The line (the \(ax + b\)) \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) b0 + b1 * x
The line in standard deviations \(z = (\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) / \sigma\) z <- (b0 + b1 * x) / sigma
Chance of being at 0 \(\Phi(-z)\) pnorm(-z)
Chance of being above 0 \(\Phi(z)\) pnorm(z)
Average among those above 0 \((\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) + \sigma\,\phi(z) / \Phi(z)\) b0 + b1 * x + sigma * dnorm(z) / pnorm(z)
Average among everybody \(\Phi(z)(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x) + \sigma\,\phi(z)\) pnorm(z) * (b0 + b1 * x) + sigma * dnorm(z)
Effect on \(y^*\) \(\beta_1\) b1
Effect on the observed \(y\) \(\beta_1\,\Phi(z)\) b1 * pnorm(z)
Effect on the chance of being above 0 \(\beta_1\,\phi(z) / \sigma\) b1 / sigma * dnorm(z)

5. Interpreting the coefficients

The Tobit slope (1.98) is the effect on the latent \(y^*\): one more hour of free time raises the desire for sport by about 2 hours. But often we want the effect on what we actually see. Two useful quantities (here \(X\beta\) is short for the line \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) of section 4):

  1. Probability of doing any sport: \(P(y > 0) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{X\beta}{\sigma}\right)\)
  2. Expected observed hours: \(E[y] = \Phi\!\left(\frac{X\beta}{\sigma}\right) X\beta + \sigma\, \phi\!\left(\frac{X\beta}{\sigma}\right)\)
Code 
sigma <- tobit$scale
xb    <- predict(tobit, grid)              # X * beta, the latent prediction
grid$p_any  <- pnorm(xb / sigma)
grid$e_hours <- pnorm(xb / sigma) * xb + sigma * dnorm(xb / sigma)
p3 <- ggplot(grid, aes(free_time, p_any)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Chance of doing any sport", x = "free time (hours per day)", y = NULL)
p4 <- ggplot(df, aes(free_time, hours)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(y = e_hours), colour = "#0082c8", linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(title = "Expected observed hours (a curve!)", x = "free time (hours per day)", y = "hours")
p3 + p4

The expected observed hours is a curve, flat near 0 (most people do nothing anyway) and close to the latent line for people with lots of free time. So the effect of one more hour of free time depends on where you are:

Code 
# average marginal effect on the observed hours: beta * P(y > 0), averaged over the people in the data
xb_people <- predict(tobit, df)
ame <- unname(coef(tobit)["free_time"]) * mean(pnorm(xb_people / sigma))
round(c(latent_effect = unname(coef(tobit)["free_time"]), effect_on_observed_hours = ame), 2)
           latent_effect effect_on_observed_hours 
                    1.98                     1.26

On average, one more hour of free time adds about 1.26 hours of observed sport, less than the latent effect, because for some people it is not enough to start doing sport at all.

Checking it with a package

The censReg package fits the same Tobit model and computes marginal effects for us (install.packages("censReg")):

Code 
library(censReg)
m <- censReg(hours ~ free_time, left = 0, data = df)
coef(m)   # same intercept and slope as survreg; logSigma is log(sigma)
(Intercept)   free_time    logSigma 
  -4.063264    1.979544    1.081779

margEff() gives the effect on the observed hours. Careful: by default it is the effect for a person with average free time (2.9 hours), not the average over all people:

Code 
summary(margEff(m))   # effect at the average free time
          Marg. Eff. Std. Error t value  Pr(>|t|)    
free_time   1.432509   0.065628  21.828 < 2.2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Read this like the coefficient table: Marg. Eff. is the effect on the observed hours, Std. Error its uncertainty, and t value and Pr(>|t|) test whether it differs from 0.

To get the average marginal effect, compute the effect for each person and take the mean. It matches the value we calculated by hand above:

Code 
each_person <- sapply(df$free_time, function(x) margEff(m, xValues = c(1, x)))   # 1 = the intercept
round(c(at_average_person = unname(margEff(m)), average_over_people = mean(each_person), by_hand = ame), 2)
  at_average_person average_over_people             by_hand 
               1.43                1.26                1.26

The two differ because the effect is not the same for everyone: it is small for people with little free time (most of them do no sport anyway) and close to 1.98 for people with a lot. The effect at the average person is not the average of the effects.

6. Reporting the results in APA style

A psychology report (APA 7th edition) needs the reason for using Tobit, the estimates with their uncertainty, the model test, and what the effect means on the observed scale. We collect the numbers from the R objects, so the text below always matches the results:

Code 
n       <- nrow(df)
n_cens  <- sum(df$hours == 0)                                  # participants at the limit
se      <- s[, "Std. Error"]
ci_low  <- s[, "Value"] - qnorm(0.975) * se                     # 95% confidence interval
ci_high <- s[, "Value"] + qnorm(0.975) * se
lr      <- 2 * diff(tobit$loglik)                               # likelihood-ratio test
lr_p    <- pchisq(lr, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
mem     <- summary(margEff(m))                                  # effect at the average person
# APA number formats: 2 decimals, p without a leading zero, "< .001" for tiny p
f2   <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pval <- function(p) if (p < .001) "< .001" else paste("=", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))

Method (data analysis):

Because 181 of the 500 participants (36.2%) reported no sport at all, weekly hours of sport were left-censored at zero. We therefore analysed them with a Tobit (censored) regression, which treats these zeros as values at or below the censoring point rather than as true zeros. Analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.6.2; R Core Team, 2026) with the survival and censReg packages.

Results:

More daily free time predicted more weekly sport, b = 1.98, SE = 0.09, z = 21.45, p < .001, 95% CI [1.80, 2.16], and the model fitted the data better than an intercept-only model, χ²(1) = 398.29, p < .001. The coefficient refers to the latent (uncensored) amount of sport: each additional hour of free time per day was associated with about 2 more hours of sport per week. On the observed scale, the average marginal effect was 1.26: averaged across participants, one more hour of free time per day was associated with 1.26 more hours of sport per week. For a participant with average free time (M = 2.94 hours), the effect was 1.43, SE = 0.07, 95% CI [1.30, 1.56].

Table 1

Tobit Regression Predicting Weekly Hours of Sport From Daily Free Time

Predictor b SE z p 95% CI
Intercept -4.06 0.35 -11.56 < .001 [-4.75, -3.37]
Free time (hours/day) 1.98 0.09 21.45 < .001 [1.80, 2.16]

Note. N = 500; 181 observations (36.2%) were left-censored at 0. σ = 2.95. Likelihood-ratio test against the intercept-only model: χ²(1) = 398.29, p < .001. Coefficients are effects on the latent outcome.

Points to remember:

  • Put statistical symbols in italics (b, SE, z, p, M); write p without a leading zero, and p < .001 for anything smaller.
  • Say why you used Tobit: how many values sit at the limit.
  • Say what the coefficient means: an effect on the latent variable.
  • Say which marginal effect you report: the average over participants, or the effect at the average participant. They differ (here 1.26 and 1.43).
  • Give 95% confidence intervals. The interval of the average marginal effect is not in the R output; get it with a bootstrap, or report only the effect at the average participant, which has an SE.
  • Cite R and the packages; citation() and citation("survival") in R give the exact references.

7. Summary

When The outcome has a pile-up at a limit (0, a maximum score, a detection limit) because values beyond it cannot be recorded
Why not OLS It treats the pile-up as real values and gives a biased, usually too flat, slope
Why not drop the zeros The remaining sample is selected, which also biases the slope
How (R) survreg(Surv(y, y > lower, type = "left") ~ x, dist = "gaussian") or AER::tobit(y ~ x, left = 0)
Interpretation Coefficients are effects on the latent \(y^*\); compute marginal effects for the observed \(y\) (censReg::margEff()), and say whether it is at the average person or averaged over people
Assumptions Normal errors with constant variance; one process decides both whether and how much
If the last assumption fails e.g. people decide separately whether to do sport and how much: use a two-part (hurdle) model
